utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Good morning, Mr. Banbury.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much: Good morning, Your Excellencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Banbury. Mr. Banbury, now we are going to be dealing with the crisis around Gorazde or the Gorazde crisis. Do you know that General Rose was in Gorazde. We did show this video here but maybe we can see it sometime. So in this footage he identified that the houses that were burned, demolished and looted were actually Serb homes that the Muslims destroyed and the -- and expelled the Serbs before the crisis?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with the footage you're -- or I don't know what footage you are talking about. Maybe I've seen it, maybe I've not, I'm not sure. But I have no doubt that there were people from the Serb community as well as the Muslim community who were affected by the crisis, their homes burned, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your statement paragraphs 13 to 15, and 23 to 25, you say what you found out, what you got in terms of information about Gorazde. Are you aware that UNPROFOR commanders objected to the one-sided and exaggerated reporting on Gorazde and that they concluded that the situation in Gorazde was not the way it was presented?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation -- the information about the situation in Gorazde was difficult to obtain because of the fighting and limited freedom of movement. We had a hard time getting a very clear realtime picture of the situation in Gorazde in April 1994. I think we had an overall understanding of it, and subsequent events or information that later became available to us that clarified the picture, I think, made it apparent that our initial overall impression was accurate. Of course, more details became available, but I don't think the fundamental understanding of UNPROFOR changed in terms of what had happened in April 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now I'm going to show a document issued by General Mladic on the basis of these rumours or Muslim propaganda.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 1D3469, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please be asked to speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Which he issued as if that was correct and later we'll see that the UNPROFOR commanders reported that the reports about the destruction and the casualties were exaggerated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you've been asked by the interpreters to speak to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Banbury, this is the 16th of April. In the English it says "probably," but I can see in the Serbian version that it is the 16th, where General Mladic personally says Muslim -- via global media, the Muslim propaganda keeps launching disinformation that the members of the VRS started a total annihilation of Muslim population in order to compromise the RS and so on and so forth. And then he orders the cruel treatments are severely forbidden as well as abuse and physical destruction of civil population, and so on and so forth. All commands and members of the VRS -- number 2, all commands and members of the VRS are duty bound to isolate and protect the civil population of Gorazde, and so on and so forth. And down at the bottom, number 5, destruction of moveable and immovable property on the liberated territory by ignition or demolition is forbidden, and so on and so forth. So is this something that fits in with what you know about the eventual actions of our command about which we also informed you at our meetings?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sorry, just before the witness answers, could we have the English version of the document just reduced a little bit so we could see the stamp. Okay, there's no translation of the stamp on the bottom and there is on the Serbian version. Thank you. Sorry, it was just a little too big, Your Honour, I wanted to see the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Dr. Karadzic, could you please just repeat the question at the very end again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I will gladly, but before that, I would like to say that this is strictly confidential and it's going through military channels. Strictly confidential. But we did inform you at meetings that we were taking these measures. Is this strictly confidential secret order in accordance with what we informed you about in our meetings?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: You and your authorities in April 1994, I believe, undertook or made a variety of representations to UNPROFOR in terms of your intentions with respect to Gorazde and the population in Gorazde. Honestly, we did not rely so much on documents or even just -- of course, commitments by any of the parties were very important to us, but we measured the behaviour of the parties, that was what was most important to us, and I think the facts that have been established with respect to Gorazde speak for themselves, and it was a very difficult time for UNPROFOR and the population of the community. It -- whatever the commitment by the -- or the orders that may have been issued, I'm sure they were respected in some cases but in others apparently they were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we admit this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't see any basis to admit this based upon the evidence just given by this witness, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As a secret document this confirms what we were speaking about publicly. We didn't conduct a two-track policy. We are saying what sort of measures we took, and therefore here is Mladic's order. So does this coincide with what we said we were going to do and undertake? Did we undertake those measures?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'd like to hear from Ms. Edgerton first, then.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think this is an argument that can be made in writing in a separate written submission about this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And there will be another opportunity for you to tender this document. Let's move on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 23 of your statement, [In English] "Weekly BH political assessment for 28th of May to 3rd of June, 1994," [Interpretation] You say that you recognise the document that you drafted and you say that you believe that the special representative managed to wrangle a commitment out of Dr. Karadzic that all armed Serb forces would be outside of the 3-kilometre exclusion zone around Gorazde. We say that that was our proposal, that those 3 kilometres, that that was our proposal. Do you allow for that possibility?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall which side first proposed the idea of a 3-kilometre exclusion zone for forces. I would have expected it would have been UNPROFOR because, as I recall, the Bosnian Serb authorities were very reluctant to move their forces back from the right side of the Drina, but it's possible, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have 65 ter 11655. 11655, and can we look at the following page. Actually, I am afraid that that is not the document. Ah, yes, the following page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we look here where it says that the authorities of Republika Srpska have decided, as a goodwill gesture, to immediately implement or facilitate the following, and then we have these items that the authorities of Republika Srpska undertook without any obligation on the Muslim side. Do you agree that this was published and that it was accepted as a goodwill gesture on our part?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that this document or these commitments were made known, whether it was a goodwill gesture or the basis for making these commitments, there had been NATO air attacks against Bosnian Serb forces, there was a lot of international pressure. I think the motivation for coming to this decision or commitment, it's probably varied. I don't believe that the undertakings made here were ever fully respected though.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, this part is a bit of subjective thinking, this part that you added. It's just guessing for your own reason?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't believe it's guessing, sir. I think it's quite clear, for instance, there was never freedom of movement for all humanitarian workers throughout the Republika Srpska, that's very clear. UNHCR was not able to operate humanitarian convoys in an unfettered nature ever throughout the course of the war, so I don't believe these -- I'm quite certain these commitments were not fully adhered to after April 18th, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I was misinterpreted. I said that this part, this added part when you say "I think," that is actually your speculation about our motives. What we have in front of us are facts and your interpretation is an attempt to guess at our motives; is that right? To say that we did that because of threats? You know we downed an aeroplane at the time. I mean, I could say that the bombing stopped because we downed an aeroplane, I mean, wouldn't that be right?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, you asked me if I agreed if this was a goodwill gesture on your part, so you are asking me to confirm the motivation for making these undertakings and based on your question, I was giving my best response as to what may have prompted you and your authorities to make these undertakings and I don't believe it was a goodwill gesture.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the first page for you to look at.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But actually, you confirmed that you did receive this text in time, on the 18th of April; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The text that's attached to this cover sheet, this is sent from UNPROFOR headquarters in Zagreb to UN headquarters in New York. I assume that it was shared with UNPROFOR headquarters in Bosnia, the Bosnia command, at the time and that I saw it, but based on this cover sheet and my recollection, I can't recall offhand, but I think it's quite likely that I saw it at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What I'm trying to do, Mr. Banbury, is to rule out your own and my own psychology, to exclude speculation and to establish the facts, and I hope that we can do that. It's a fact that that day we sent out and we said publicly that this was a goodwill gesture, but you if you have doubts about it, then that's your thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, let's not waste time anymore. There's no doubt the document says goodwill on your part, but it's a separate matter whether the witness would agree with it or not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we admit this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1152, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said that one of your activities was to interpret the UNPROFOR mandate to your colleagues; is that right? That that was a part of your job?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct, interpreting it in more of a political sense or translating what the mandate said into the current operating environment or when confronted with a situation. I was not responsible for giving a legal interpretation of the mandate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree or is it something that is understandable and acceptable to you that Serbs responded to offensives from safe areas and that specifically this crisis in Gorazde was caused by the actions of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina from the Gorazde safe area?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly agree that there were many times when the Bosnian Serb Army was responding to offensive actions by the Bosnian Army, the Bosnian government army. I do not necessarily agree that the actions in Gorazde were in response only to Bosnian government forces' actions, and it's a whole separate matter of what was justified or allowed under the safe area mandate. So I think it gets complicated very fast.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we just briefly have D687, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is from the same day. You and two of your colleagues drafted this telegram from Mr. Andreev, your boss, to Mr. Akashi. Would you agree that was sent on the 18th of April and that you are one of the authors of this document?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page 2, please, paragraph 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It states: [In English] "The council must clarify the concept of the safe areas as soon as possible. Until now, they have never been geographically defined and it has never been clear how UNPROFOR was meant to deter attacks on them or whether indeed UNPROFOR should have tolerated their use by the Bosnian Army for military purposes. If the council decides to continue with the concept, it must be willing to give the resources and the political commitment necessary do so. Otherwise, we invite conflict with the Serbs for no benefit to anyone." [Interpretation] This relates to this crisis, your service, the head of the civilians affairs section is asking for a clarification of the concept of the safe areas because the Bosnian Army was abusing it. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do agree that on this occasion and others we sought clarification of the safe area concept. We sought it for many reasons. I don't necessarily agree that the Bosnian Army was abusing it in this case, that's a separate matter. And in part because of lack of clarification, the concept of abuse or not was subjective.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you agree that this dispatch of the 18th of April was on the topic of the crisis in Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 1D02548.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a statement by Mr. Zametica who talks about -- well, you can look at this here: [In English] "If air-strikes continue, we shall find ourselves at war with the United Nations," says Zametica." [Interpretation] Then he continues on to explain that the Army of Republika Srpska was not shelling Gorazde and that members of humanitarian organisations and members of UNPROFOR cannot be in any danger. And then it continues: [In English] "Muslim war propaganda launches new fabrications from Gorazde which dangerously fuel reckless decisions about the combat use of NATO air force and contributes to the escalation of the war." [Interpretation] And so on and so forth. You can see this whole statement. Do you remember our warnings that this was a trap here and a propaganda and exaggeration?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall those warnings. I also know that we had personnel in Gorazde who were providing realtime reporting about events that were taking place in and around Gorazde and those reports were at times at odds with press dispatches from Belgrade or, indeed, representations from Pale.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we admit this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it will be admitted given that the alleged speaker, Mr. Zametica, was the spokesman for the Presidency at the time. I think we have basis to admit it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1153, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have D137 for a minute, please. D137. It's also a United Nations document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is from July 1995, at the time when you were performing these duties in Zagreb where the headquarters of Mr. Akashi were.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page 6 now, please. This is a document sent by General Janvier. Can we now look at the third paragraph from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] "Similar to what happened in Gorazde spring 1994, the BH can attempt to draw UNPROFOR, including the rapid reaction forces or NATO, into the conflict on the BH side. Sudden abandoning of positions along the confrontation line, the simulation of a collapse of the enclave or alarming reports from the Bosnian side on the situation in the enclave will be indicators for this. A stronger involvement of the international community could be interpreted by the Bosnian Serb Army as an incentive to step up operations and try to eliminate the enclave, as well as retaliate against the UN forces." [Interpretation] So, Mr. Banbury, General Janvier took this as a model of behaviour by the Muslim side when they want to draw NATO in as well as the UN and the international community, to draw them into a war. They pretend that the enclave had collapsed, reports that are sent are exaggerated, and these reports are alarming, saying that everything is disastrous. Do you remember that that was General Janvier's position and that that is what he wrote in this telegram of his?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I may, we've been through this with documents like this before, Your Honour. This is not a document from General Janvier. This is a UNPF, United Nations Protection Force headquarters daily sitrep drafted by someone other than General Janvier, released by someone other than General Janvier, and representing that something this anything produced by General Janvier is actually a misrepresentation. And with respect, that's evident on the front page of the document, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the first page again? Although this has already been admitted. Can we have the first page? It says there: "From General Janvier."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I would direct everyone's attention to the drafter's name, to the releasing officer's name, to the signature block. It may come from the office of General Janvier, but it can't be representative as General Janvier's document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: A document in the name of General Janvier. Let us proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have 65 ter 21146.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did we hear your question and answer from the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did put a question but I don't know whether Mr. Banbury gave an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So at that point in time you were in Zagreb; right?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know that there were such views in the UN about the crisis in Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of those views. There were such views within the UN Protection Force headquarters in some -- among some military officers and perhaps civilians. I think they represented a minority view and they were subsequently largely discredited.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. With all due respect, Mr. Banbury, I think that minority and majority pertains to matters related to democratic life in a society, but these are two generals that held this view; right? Please, for the transcript, nodding is not reflected in the transcript, so could you speak up and tell us what your position is?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that in this case, though General Janvier had those concerns, I don't think they reflect the entirety of his views but he certainly -- he and some of his officers had those concerns, and those concerns on the part of General Janvier did influence his actions. And I think not just senior UN leadership in UNPROFOR but also in UN headquarters later, with the benefit of hindsight, believed that General Janvier's actions based in part on those views turned out to be disastrous for the organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But, Mr. Banbury, this is from July 1995, a year and two months after that. So this is a view that was held, and do you agree the General Rose had this same view and that General Janvier based his views on opinions from the ground because he was not in Gorazde; right?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The possibility or risk that the Bosnian government and its army would try and act in a way to have UNPROFOR act in a way that would be favourable to their cause was present throughout the conflict. Of course the Bosnian government, the Bosnian military wanted us, wanted UNPROFOR to act in a way that would advance their cause and not act counter to it. I think the Bosnian Serb authorities had the exact same interest, that we would act in a way that would advance their cause or did not, at the least, harm it. Both sides were constantly trying to influence the behaviour of UNPROFOR. In the case of this risk that the Bosnian government army would act in a way to draw UNPROFOR into armed conflict with the Bosnian Serbs in the safe areas, we were aware that -- of that possibility, of that risk. I, myself, and -- well, I don't want to speak for my colleagues, but I, myself, do not believe that the Bosnian government army acted in a way to sacrifice their civilians in order to have UNPROFOR call in NATO air-strikes. I think there was a real conflict in Gorazde, there was a real conflict in Srebrenica and the military aspects of both those conflicts are multidimensional, I won't try to analyse them here, but I acknowledge that the risk existed. We were aware of it at the time. We paid close attention to it. We based our actions on the entirety of the situation on the ground according to our best understanding.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have 65 ter 21146. Let us see what another general says about the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 25th of April. It is General De Lapresle who is sending this directly to Kofi Annan in New York. One: [In English] "The situation in Gorazde has stabilised as the BSA forces have completed their withdrawal from the 3-kilometre line agreed upon between Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Akashi in Belgrade. This phase of the operation is now complete." [Interpretation] Number 3: [In English] "The military situation on the ground in Gorazde is much improved, although sporadic small arms fire is present from time to time. For their part, the BH forces have not been helpful in targeting the withdrawing Serbs with sniper fire. At least, 13 BSA casualties resulted along the east-west road to Ustipraca. The BSA prepared an armoured counterattack but did not execute it and eventually withdrew their forces."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us look at number 6: [In English] "As soon as BSA withdrawal is complete, I believe that we must focus our attention on two other aspects of the overall problem. The first of these is that of the other safe areas, their definition and our concept of operations with respect to them." [Interpretation] The last sentence: [In English] "I fear that unless the Bosnian Serbs and the BH are brought together in the negotiating process, then we will be faced with another outbreak of intense conflict, initiated by one party or the other." [Interpretation] Does this general instill confidence in you?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Does General De Lapresle instill confidence in me? Not really.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's a good thing that you are not a military man. But Mr. Banbury, look at the first page, they hit 13 of our men as we were withdrawing. Is that permitted?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they ought not to have done that and there were many instances when the Bosnian government army acted in a way that we did not want them to, that we had asked them not to. I think this is -- you know, this was a war and the sides acted in their interest, not according to UNPROFOR requests. In this case, the -- at this time late April 1994, after the attack in Gorazde, the NATO air power, the plane being downed, the territorial gains made by the Bosnian Serb Army, the Bosnian government, the Bosnian Army were bitterly and deeply disappointed in UNPROFOR's behaviour and believe we had capitulated to pressure from the Bosnian Serbs and that we had relented and acquiesced to gains that they found unacceptability. They were very angry at us and I think they acted in a way to reflect their interest not ours. I think this report also shows again that we factually and accurately reported the true situation on the ground according to the best of our understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1154, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D3419, could we have that, please. We are still in April 1994, and this has to do with Gorazde. So this is the 27th of April. Can we look at the next page?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We see the part that has been marked here, it says that the situation was becoming stable, that the Serbs withdrew, Serb elements had withdrawn except for two locations where equipment has been disabled and that confirms an assessment that the BSA intends to comply with the ultimatum. No BSA -- oh, no BSA forces remained in the 3-kilometre zone around Gorazde. "There was, however, an incident initiated by the BH who fired 50 small arms [In English] rounds at an UNPROFOR patrol from the position west of the Drina River. A strong protest was lodged to the BH command."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This firing at UNPROFOR, Mr. Banbury, does it look like frustration to you, as it does to me, because shooting at UNPROFOR in a situation like this means trying to provoke UNPROFOR; right?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that the shooting at UNPROFOR by the Bosnian Army reflect -- likely reflected frustration on their part and whether it was mere frustration or designed to provoke a response by us, I don't know. But certainly frustration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to draw your attention to this passage that is marked that says that the assessment is that the efforts made are being sincere and that it's the potential for BH Army attacks that is probably their main concern, since the Bosniaks, the Muslims, have not signed an agreement yet which they would be bound to comply with. Do you agree that the Serb side here -- or rather, that it was reported that the Serb side here was sincerely complying, although the Muslim side hadn't signed this yet, and that this caused concern among the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I note this is a document from the international conference on the former Yugoslavia, not UNPROFOR. These were -- this was a diplomatic conference not a peacekeeping mission. They did not have any presence on the ground, so I think this is thirdhand reporting. The -- I also agree, though, that the Bosnian Serbs at this point in late April were complying with -- were complying with some of the commitments they had undertaken, were generally compliant with the pull-back from Gorazde and the cessation of the attack on Gorazde. There were a number of commitments that we had sought and that we either made and not respected or were not made at all. I don't agree, for instance, that all Bosnian Serb forces had pulled back from the right side of the Drina. We know that, as reported in UNPROFOR documents, that some Bosnian Serb forces had changed into civilian clothes and maintained their weapons in the 3-kilometre zone. As for the Bosnian government not having signed an agreement that they were honour-bound to comply, we were not asking the Bosnian government to sign an agreement. They -- it was a safe area that was being attacked by the Bosnian Serbs. We were asking the Bosnian Serbs to stop the attack and withdraw.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, that is precisely what we are going to discuss now. First of all, it is our claim that this was a Serb counter-attack. Do you agree that it was a Serb counter-attack?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think in a sustained war across a large conflict line it's very difficult to distinguish between attack and counter-attack. What -- there may be an attack in one area and the counter-attack may occur at a point of weakness along someone's lines 100 kilometres away, but for the people 100 kilometres away, that counter-attack may appear as an attack. So I think it's very hard to characterise what amounts to an attack or a counterattack. I think it's much easier to characterise what the obligations were with respect to the safe areas. Notwithstanding the fact that the concept was never clarified to the point that we would have liked, there were still some very obvious obligations with respect to the safe area concept, and so I -- I don't want to go on because your question didn't ask me that, but that's my view with respect to attack or counter-attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. During the interview we agreed that the Serb army consisted of the local population. Do you agree that these people who were liberating right bank were actually freeing their own homes and they stayed at their homes as they were wearing civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we agreed or I agreed during the interview that the Bosnian Serb Army had members within it including those fighting in areas very close to their original homes and that could have an impact on their feelings. With respect to the -- the soldiers in the Bosnian Serb Army that were fighting in Gorazde, in and around Gorazde in April 1994, I, myself, do not know the composition of those forces but I certainly acknowledge the possibility that some of the forces were originally from that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm going to put a document before you that unfortunately has not been translated yet. It has been sent out to be translated, though.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, can the previous document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1155, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I draw your attention and the attention of all the participants to paragraph 24 of your statement, which says that you were shown a document that refers to Mladic's order that VRS soldiers within a 3-kilometre zone should change into civilian clothes. And then your interpretation is, I'm going to read it out in English: [In English] "This is consistent with my recollection of Bosnian Serb behaviour toward international agreements during this period. As the document demonstrates, they were both audacious and arrogant, they thought they could get away with everything." [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Banbury, is this not a bit of a sign of ill will towards the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, I think there was tremendous ill will shown by the Bosnian Serbs toward UNPROFOR, and there were countless commitments made to us that were not respected and I don't believe there was ever any intention to respect them at the time they were made, so my -- I never had any ill will to any party in the conflict. I did have views toward the parties with respect to how they treated UNPROFOR and how they conducted themselves in the conflict. I don't think this shows ill will, I think that reflected the situation at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But the soldiers remaining in that zone was something that had been agreed upon with the UN, that they would stop being soldiers, that they should change into civilian clothes and that they should protect their homes and families by way of their own presence. The document that confirms this is 1D2991. It seems to me that you haven't actually been told everything and that you did not really know about everything from the military sphere; right?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am certainly sure that I was not told everything and am not aware of everything that happened in the military sphere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We haven't received the translation yet but I shall read this, not all of it, just the first line: "On the 27th of April, 1994, at a joint meeting between the representatives of the VK RS with the representatives of the United Nations, Mr. de Mello and General Soubirou, it was stated that the cease-fire agreement in Gorazde had been attained and an agreement reached between Mr. Akashi and President Karadzic was fully carried out in accordance with what had been agreed upon and Security Council Resolution 913. The representatives of the UN had only two minor objections. Namely, first of all, that not all soldiers of the VRS were removed from the zone of 3 kilometres on the right bank, and the zone from the villages of Gornje Kolijevke and Rahla, and secondly, that in the zone of the right bank of the river, there is an enormous number of RS policemen and that they were treating UNPROFOR arrogantly." The next paragraph says, it was agreed -- it was agreed that soldiers of the VRS shall wear civilian clothes in the mentioned areas with the explanation that these are local persons who have no other clothing because their village had been razed to the ground by the Muslims. It was also agreed upon that part of the policemen who are locals would change into civilian clothing and that all problems with UNPROFOR would be resolved by way of agreement. Can we look at the last page, it says "Strictly confidential." On the first page it says "Strictly confidential, very urgent," there is a code number as well. And on the last page it says "Major-General Milan Gvero," who attended this meeting with Mr. de Mello and General Soubirou on behalf of General Mladic. Had you known about this agreement, your assessment regarding the presence of these soldiers that were turned into civilians would have been different, probably; right?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not agree with the characterisation of the agreement. I am aware that, from the UNPROFOR perspective, we agreed with the Bosnian Serb authorities that military or police personnel could stay in the 3-kilometre zone on the right bank of the Drina if they not only took off their uniform, if they left those forces. They were not supposed to be -- if they left the military, they left the police, they became civilians, then of course they could stay in their homes. They could not simply take off their uniforms and continue conducting themselves as members of the forces, of the military or police forces. The key distinction for us was that they had to leave the police force or the military. And as is clear here, the -- the Bosnian Serb authorities had a very different interpretation, in my view probably a deliberate one, which was to evade the obligation to get their forces out of the 3-kilometre zone. The idea wasn't what clothes they were wearing and the ruse that they -- all their civilian clothes were gone, we never believed that for a moment. Despite being told that at the time, we never believed that. Our interest was to get all Bosnian Serb forces, no matter what clothes they were wearing, outside of the 3-kilometre zone. This document here makes clear that the Bosnian Serbs were trying to get around that obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree, Mr. Banbury, that when a man comes and frees his home after two years, that you don't have the heart or the right to send him away from there? Do you agree that it's a very sensitive issue? You don't have the right to send him away from there and you don't have the heart to do it either?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree it's a very sensitive issue. It was a very, very difficult issue for the Serb population on the right bank of the Drina. Nonetheless, it was the UNPROFOR view that there needed to be a withdrawal of all Serb forces from a 3-kilometre zone. We decided that we should allow men to stay behind, including with their weapons if they chose to, but the condition for them staying behind was that they had to leave the military or police forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we admit this for identification only, and the translation is coming soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll mark it for identification pending English translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D1156, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 1D3420, please. This is a document of the UNPROFOR Zagreb HQ of the 6th of May, 1994. Can we look at the fifth page from this one, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you look at this assessment and look at this part that is boxed in: [In English] "The BiH apparently attempted to provoke an incident between the BSA and an element of Ukrainian Battalion 2. However, the arrival and deployment of additional troops will help maintain order in the town as well as ensure enforcement of UN resolutions." [Interpretation] Do you agree that as early as May, the 6th of May, after all of our withdrawals, the Bosnia-Herzegovina Army was trying to cause a conflict between the Serbs and the Ukrainian battalion and that this was remarked upon by the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The report says "apparently attempted to provoke an incident." I am personally not familiar with that incident, whether it was ever confirmed that that was the intention. So I have a hard time commenting on that particular incident.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 10 of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you look at this document where they are informing about convoys, and then it says three convoys were turned back by the Serbs that were going to Srebrenica. So this would then be part of the report that Serbs were creating obstacles for the convoys; is that correct? Two were refused for Gorazde and three for Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's information that conveys some of the problems, a very small portion of the problems we had with respect to our convoys to Srebrenica and Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This table doesn't state anything about the reasons, does it?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you would recall from the previous page that there was an incident there caused by the B&H Army between the Serbs and the Ukrainians in relation to Gorazde, this is what we were reading a bit earlier?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The report referred to an apparent effort to provoke an incident, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at the last page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here is the summary [In English] of convoys requested from headquarters Pale for 6th of May, 1994. [Interpretation] Confirmations 16, refusals 4, no answer none, and so on and so forth. So 20 per cent were refused. Can you look at the bottom, please, what it says in paragraph 2, DutchBat number so and so: [In English] "The Muslim forces have not ceased their combat activities onto the RS territory. Until yet you have nothing done to prevent this activities. Whatever reasons you may have, your safety on the RS territory is in that way directly endangered." [Interpretation] So we have confirmation that those two convoys for Gorazde were stopped because of an incident, and now we have confirmation that the three that were stopped that were going to Srebrenica for the reason that the Muslim side was carrying out attacks on Republika Srpska territory from Srebrenica, because DutchBat was in Srebrenica, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am sorry, Dr. Karadzic, I don't agree that we have confirmation those are the reasons the convoys were blocked because of the incident or the alleged incident in Gorazde or because the Bosnian government forces in Srebrenica were engaged in combat activities. With all due respect, I think it was UNPROFOR's decision, not the Bosnian Serbs, to decide whether or not our convoys were to proceed to the safe areas or to the enclaves in the east. It was a very clear and unambiguous obligation on the part of the Bosnian Serb authorities to let our convoys proceed based on the Security Council resolutions and the obligations with respect to our freedom of movement. The Bosnian Serbs came up with a million different reasons to block our convoys. In our view, none were ever acceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After the break we are going to deal with the convoys. All I wanted to say was that this document, the table, does not give any reasons, and then we can see in the rest of the document reasons are given that could be taken into consideration. But, Mr. Banbury, every time rejection of a convoy received an explanation, an explanation was given. Isn't it correct that the Serbs did state their reasons? Regardless of whether you accept that or not, the Serbs gave a reason, the reason was either your security or the security or safety of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was normal practice for the Bosnian Serbs to give a reason for the rejection. It was not always the case that we received a reason, but the point is there was never, ever, a case where any of those reasons were viewed as acceptable by UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But you do not dispute, in any event, that it was our right to determine the conditions under which convoys would move through our territory, through our lines, I'm talking about humanitarian aid and other forms of aid? I mean, we did have the right to do that under the Geneva Conventions; no?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree entirely with that proposition. The Security Council made very clear in its resolutions that UNPROFOR and humanitarian organisations were entitled to total freedom of movement, and it was not up to the Bosnian Serb authorities at all to restrict our freedom of movement. That was a consistent violation of the obligations of the Bosnian Serbs. Nor was it UNPROFOR's obligation to provide justification for our convoys. The entire convoy regime was totally inconsistent with the obligations imposed upon the parties by the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Banbury, we don't have time to look at the Geneva Conventions and other documents that predate UN Security Council resolutions that give us the right to approve and to inspect, but if we have time we will show it. We did tender the Geneva Convention, that section of it that regulates that question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we admit this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1157, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 1D3421, please. 1D3421.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That wasn't one of the 152 documents we received notification on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I ask for your kind understanding. Perhaps it just slipped through. We did have the intention to candidate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Has it been uploaded?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think it has been released. So shall you move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We will come back to that then. It has been uploaded. We will see it in a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is the 11th of May, from Andreev to Akashi. It's an analysis of the evolving relationship between the B&H government and UNPROFOR. Can you please look at the third paragraph: [In English] "The sense of frustration was much greater following the virtual repeat of the Sarajevo experience in Gorazde. It is apparent that certain circles within the BH government, probably led by Prime Minister Silajdzic, put much at stake politically in their gamble in Gorazde. The evolution of events created heightened expectations, false ones as it turned out, that finally the international community was going to enter into the conflict as a combatant on the BH side. These expectations were passed on to the population through inflammatory statements by the BH officials, and often biased press reports." [Interpretation] And a little bit lower: [In English] "The BH again failed to obtain what is perhaps its primary short-term objective, despite having been so close." [Interpretation] Can we look at the following page. [In English] "The comments coming from BH government directed primarily against the special representative of Secretary-General needs to be seen. These comments, including calls for the special representative resignation, are an attempt by the BH government to assign blame for its own inability to draw the international community into the conflict as a combatant." [Interpretation] And the next paragraph: [In English] "... because it is politically untenable to assert as an objective the participation of the UN/NATO as combatants in the conflict, a pretext was needed. The transit of BSA tanks through the Sarajevo total exclusion zone is simply being exploited by the BH in its quest to divert the attention and blame for the failure to draw the international community into the conflict on the BH side." [Interpretation] And the last page. The last page, please. The last paragraph at the bottom, the last two sentences: [In English] "... were the population to have a better understanding of UNPROFOR's proper role, as defined by the UN Security Council, public opinion might be less subject to manipulation in ways detrimental to our work on the ground." [Interpretation] Was this something that the chief of your civilian sector sent, during the time that you were there, to Akashi, and were these the concerns of the civilian sector?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Andreev sent that to Mr. Akashi at a time when I was working with Mr. Andreev in Sarajevo and I think the document does reflect some of Mr. Andreev's concerns.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we admit this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1158, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 1D3422.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If you agree, this is a self-explanatory document. It explains itself so I didn't want to analyse it any further. We have to save time. Do you agree that this is a document sent from Annan to Akashi on the 23rd of May, 1994, and it relates to the situation in Gorazde; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at the document and then I'm going to introduce the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the following page, please, if you've read this one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have not read the second paragraph yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I can help a little bit.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that Mr. Annan is aware that the media are ready to distort the picture? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think Mr. Annan and UN officials in general were well aware that the media did not always accurately depict events on the ground, yeah. That's a constant problem with the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can we now look at the highlighted portions of the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There is an objection by Mr. Gharekhan here and he states: [In English] "I should like to inform you that on 21st of May, following several hours of negotiations laid by the force commander, General de Lapresle, an agreement was signed by General Rose with General Milovanovic of the Serb military leadership relating to the situation in and around Gorazde. In principal points of this agreement as -- the principal points of this agreement are as follows ..." [Interpretation] And now we can all look at the bullet points. And it states here, the second paragraph from this one, that the agreement is to be signed by the government of the army -- by the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina and it is also meant to oblige the local Bosnian Army commander not to undertake any offensive actions or forward troop movements into this area. And then the next paragraph states: "However, the government side has so far refused to sign the agreement." So you did, after all, ask the government to sign the agreement, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is at the end of May in 1994 and it was a different situation and a different time than in April 1994, but in this case, yes, we were asking the Bosnian government to undertake certain commitments with respect to Gorazde, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It states here: [In English] "However, the government side so far refused to sign an agreement which has therefore not yet come into effect." [Interpretation] And then lower down: [In English] "BSA forces have withdrawn from the north side of the river Drina. Forces of the army of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina attempted to move to these vacated positions, but UNPROFOR did not permit them to do so. UNPROFOR itself will deploy in this area." [Interpretation] And the last paragraph on this page: [In English] "There are misleading press reports about Serbs reinforcing within the 3-kilometre zone. These are incorrect. In fact, there is no change within 3-kilometre zone, but outside it, at the confrontation line, they have withdrawn in some areas and reinforced their positions in others." [Interpretation] Do you know Mr. Gharekhan, and do you know about these issues?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know Mr. Gharekhan and, yes, I'm familiar with these issues.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1159, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now briefly look at D707. It's already been admitted. I just would like Mr. Banbury to see what the other side is doing at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a document of the Muslim side and the topic is Gorazde. I assume that there is a translation because -- yes. You can see here after this operation career and with the intention of getting some activities going: "In order to alleviate the situation in Podrinje and create the basic prerequisites for a long-term resolution of this complex problem, I hereby propose, 1, urgently organise the 8th Corps, (including the units in Srebrenica, Zepa, and Operations Group Pazaric) as announced." Then four names are propose for possible commanders. "The above-named commander should take a group of officers to Gorazde and a unit that should have at least 200 well-equipped soldiers."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at paragraph 4: "Significant financial support should be approved and they should be taught to use UNPROFOR as a supplier." And then deliver MTS especially for anti-armour combat to them with special transport, and so on and so forth. Mr. Banbury, would this be the reason for the concern of the Army of Republika Srpska regarding the transports entering the safe areas? This is an instruction from the highest levels to instruct the forces how to use the presence of UNPROFOR for purposes of procurement or supply?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can understand the concern. I don't know what they are referring to in paragraph 4, but yes, I can understand the concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I draw your attention to what Mr. Izetbegovic wrote at the bottom. I agree more or less with everything except item 2, which refers to the commanders, but he does agree with everything else. And that is the reason, Mr. Banbury, why the Serbian Army must control and impose restrictions regarding the materiel that could possibly be used against it. This is the duty and the task of every army. First of all, to take care of its own security. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the UNPROFOR perspective, the primary duties and obligations came from the Security Council resolutions, and the Security Council resolutions demanded that all parties provide UNPROFOR with freedom of movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We would agree in the -- in your interview and you also mention that at other occasions that I, as the civilian head of state and the army, was not informed about tactical matters. Do you agree that the civilian head must not conclude any agreement that would jeopardise the security of his own army and that he has to allow his officers to do that?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's normal that the civilian -- that the head of the civilian authority would not normally be involved in tactical military issues or agreements related to tactical matters. What is tactical, what is strategic is a separate issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it time for the break or should I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll have a break for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Banbury, we have to move away from the issue of Gorazde because there are many other topics we need to cover. Therefore, I wish to remind you that in many paragraphs of your statement, such as 16, 33, 43, 44, 65, 69, and 71, through to 172, you dealt a lot with humanitarian issues such as utilities, UNPROFOR's freedom of movement, the airport, and blue and other routes. Due to a lack of time, I will try to summarise because this is all to the detriment of Defence, but I will try to summarise as much as I can. First of all, I wish to present you a document, it's D143, which gives an overview of the movement of convoys in the year 1994. D143. Please read it, I do not wish to read it, I will just summarise so that we can save some time. As you can see, this is an overview of convoys for the year 1994 and it says here which check-points they passed through and what were the elements and on the basis of what these convoys were searched.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please see the next page now. Here we can see there's a section about behaviour and abuse of mandate by UNPROFOR. Can we also turn to the next page in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please have a look, I will read this for you: "In 1994, as previously, checks mostly revealed the following attempts at abuse: Transport of goods which are not permitted at all in UNPROFOR convoys, transport of goods which do not constitute humanitarian aid in convoys of humanitarian organisations, transport of goods in quantities greater than those permitted." Anyone can read it. Please let's look at the passage beginning with the word "understandably": "Understandably, most cases of attempted smuggling of goods were in the convoys for Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde ..." And it's then mentioned what was most often smuggled, video cameras, cameras, weapons, radios, satellite equipment and antennas, signal equipment, optical instruments, instruments for recording during the night, gear oil, anti-freeze, oxygen bottles, protective vests, helmets and on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please move on to the next page in Serbian. There is no doubt that there would have been very few attempts to smuggle non-permitted goods if these had been confiscated permanently at the check-points. It was confiscated but then it was also given back when the convoys returned. Then the person who is making the analysis says that it would have been better if it had been confiscated permanently because then there would have been fewer attempts to smuggle these goods. Can we now please see the table which is at the end of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here is the overview, these are thousands of tonnes, for example, the first one: 5.051 tonnes of flour, 381 tonnes of beans, and so on and so forth. Sugar, 180 tonnes and so on. Were you informed, Mr. Banbury, that goods which were not reported were smuggled in these convoys and which do not belong to the sort of goods that the UNPROFOR needed?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this document reflects very well the fundamental problem and disagreement between UNPROFOR and the Bosnian Serb authorities, on the one hand, and also UNPROFOR and UNHCR with respect to humanitarian goods. The document characterises goods that are not permitted and lists things like weapons, optical devices, oxygen bottles. It was UNPROFOR's absolute belief or conviction that we were allowed to transport weapons for personnel, our military personnel into Srebrenica, that we were allowed to bring in optical devices like binoculars, also radio sets. These are standard, basic, military equipment that you -- the United Nations provides to its peacekeepers around the world, and in my current role as Assistant Secretary-General for Field Support I'm responsible for in part providing UN peacekeeping forces with equipment around the world. This is basic, standard equipment for UN peacekeepers. The notion that they are not permitted was purely a -- something manufactured by the Bosnian Serbs. We never agreed to it. And it was an absolute violation of their responsibilities under the Security Council mandate to block such goods from going in. The question with respect to -- and I also note that oxygen bottles were called unpermitted goods. Oxygen was there to treat wounded soldiers or soldiers who had some type of medical problem and could have an important role in stabilising them pending a medical evacuation. I also know for a fact that there were many times when medical evacuation requests for UN soldiers in the enclaves were denied by Bosnian Serbs and requests to evacuate people by helicopter were denied and we had to bring in an ambulance which meant extra hours and hours until the soldiers were able to receive proper medical care. Oxygen could be the difference between life and death. So the notion that somehow the Bosnian Serbs had the right to determine that oxygen was not permitted into the enclaves for UN medical purposes for our soldiers, I find totally unacceptable. With respect to the humanitarian assistance, I also, as was indicated in the very opening of my appearance here, served for six years as the Asia regional director for the United Nations World Food Programme, a humanitarian organisation. I believe it is the role of humanitarian organisations to determine what is humanitarian assistance, as well as the quantities required to provide for the civilian population in an area where they are in need of assistance. So I do not agree at all that items that UNHCR characterised as humanitarian assistance could be determined otherwise by the Bosnian Serb authorities. And I also do not agree at all that the quantities required, as determined by UNHCR, were somehow subject to a separate determination on the part of the Bosnian Serb authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you know that the agreement was that this had to be reported, so why were the goods not listed on a declaration form but then, rather, there were oxygen bottles that were full of gun powder? Do you know that oxygen bottles were used for smuggling explosives in humanitarian and UNPROFOR convoys and usually these bottles were not even listed on the declaration form?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not an agreement that the items would be listed on the declaration form. It was a requirement imposed by the Bosnian Serb authorities under protests from the United Nations because we had no choice but to comply with, in my view, unjust obligations imposed by the Bosnian Serb authorities with respect to the convoys. We did list the -- the material on the convoys. It's entirely possible that because of the very onerous bureaucratic requirements that were imposed upon us, the huge number of convoys providing logistical support, food, fuel, ammunition, weapons, et cetera, for large military contingents is a huge operation, complex logistical operation, with many -- and I do this now professionally, this is my job. There's a lot of material, spare parts, et cetera, et cetera. I'm sure that because of the detailed nature of the bureaucratic requirements that were at the insistence of the Bosnian Serb authorities, no doubt UNPROFOR made some errors at times and didn't include everything that ended up on a convoy. What was prepared on a piece of paper 48 hours earlier in one location and what was put on the convoys at another location 48 hours later, when the soldiers were getting ready to go, and they hadn't included something, it's entirely -- in fact I would say inevitable that mistakes were made, honest mistake without any ill intention. As for the proposition that oxygen bottles were used to smuggle gun powder or explosives, I'm unaware of any case of that and I don't believe that UNPROFOR intentionally smuggled gun powder in an oxygen bottle ever once during the course of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll have an occasion to see that and we already had one. But can you please tell me this: Do you want to say that the UNPROFOR and UNHCR did not smuggle goods that were not permitted and that these convoys were not abused in order to supply our opponents, the other warring party, with war materiel? You can just answer that with yes or no, if you don't mind?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not agree that there were goods that were permitted or not permitted from the UNPROFOR perspective, so the notion that UNPROFOR or UNHCR smuggled non-permitted goods is not a proposition that I can accept because it was up to UNPROFOR, on the one hand, and UNHCR, on the other, to determine what was necessary for the conduct of our responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you deny that one warring party which allows transportation to cross through its territory and its lines to set the conditions under which this would be done, would you deny that this is part of the Geneva Conventions, I thinks protocol 3, which allows a warring party to determine that? Is a warring party which lets convoys pass through allowed to determine the conditions? Don't speak as an American now but, rather, as a representative the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not an expert on the Geneva Conventions. I do know that the Geneva Conventions do not apply to UNPROFOR. This was with respect -- Geneva Conventions applied to humanitarian assistance. The Security Council, acting under Chapter 7 of the United Nations Charter, which can oblige member states to act in a certain way and create binding legal international obligations on parties, made very clear that UNPROFOR was to be -- and UNHCR were to be entitled freedom of movement to carry out their responsibilities. We were never granted that freedom of movement including with respect to the convoys in the case of Bosnian Serb territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Banbury, freedom of movement was provided but not without control and this is our misunderstanding. You think more like an American, that you are allowed to do whatever you want, wherever you come, but you cannot -- in a sovereign state, you cannot act differently than it was agreed on the basis of various norms. Geneva Conventions are more important here than resolutions of the Security Council, isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer, yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's argumentative and not an appropriate remark to make with respect to this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, it's all of those things and it's also an attempt by the back door to give evidence yet again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Nevertheless, I trust that the witness is able to answer the question. Do you remember the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can read it on the transcript, Your Honour. Dr. Karadzic, the restrictions imposed upon UNPROFOR and UNHCR for our activities on territory controlled by the Bosnian Serb authorities were never subject to an agreement. They were constantly under protest by UNPROFOR and UNHCR and indeed at higher levels. The obligations created by Security Council resolutions were paramount and they imposed the requirement for the parties to provide UNPROFOR with full freedom of movement. They repeatedly -- several resolutions insisted upon the access by humanitarian organisations, unfettered access by humanitarian organisations to populations in need. Those obligations were not respected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The misunderstanding will relate to unlimited access, whether there was control or not. Please don't be angry with me. I envy you because, as an American, you can think as you do. I did not wish to be insulting when I made remarks about Americans.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have a look briefly at D695 so that we can see that this was a subject of communication constantly between Mr. Akashi and myself. The document is D695.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at this letter which I address to Mr. Akashi on the 24th of June, 1994. And where it says that there was such abuse and also the freedom of movement is discussed, as well as the relations with the Republika Srpska. [In English] "I need hardly remind you that the recent Geneva agreement has provided for cessation of hostilities and the exchange of prisoners. The Muslims are completely ignoring their signature over this agreement." [Interpretation] And a bit lower: [In English] "Apart from this, UNPROFOR forces take little notice of the agreed procedure (for example, undecided [sic] goods and equipment) and display unacceptable behaviour, as if they are an enemy [sic] of occupation. What is even worse, UNPROFOR is allowing the Muslims to use its observation posts and there have been many occasions when the blue helmets have used artillery to fire at Serb positions. I ask you to use your influence in order for UNPROFOR to act in a manner that will inspire Serb confidence. But I shall do everything in my power to remove any obstacles of the freedom of movement of UNPROFOR. Equally, as we are in a very delicate phase, I would like to ask you to try to ensure that no unnecessary problems are being created by UNPROFOR." [Interpretation] You can see still today that we would continue to have misunderstanding not before [as interpreted] one or the other side was evil, but because there was a misunderstanding concerning the mandate. Would you agree that we agreed to your presence under one specific mandate? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that you ever really agreed to our presence. In some respects you did and in some respects you didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you couldn't have been there if we hadn't given our approval. And do you know that our request was that you could not change the initial mandate without our approval?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that was the view, your view and the view of the Bosnian Serb authorities, but the mandate was not a question for UNPROFOR, it was only a matter to be determined by the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please see D966 just for a short time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As we are dealing with humanitarian issues, please focus on this one, it's the 29th of June, 1994. It's a weekly situation report sent by Mr. Akashi to Mr. Annan.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can we now please see page 4 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You can look at the first frame, Sarajevo averaged and so on. We can see that the Muslim side violated the cease-fire by targeting Serbian position and that the Serbian Army was restraining from responding. Were you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was probably aware of that incident at that time. I, at this time, do not recall offhand that particular incident, but I assume that it took place as described in the UNPROFOR document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have page 6, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here it is. I will read something which begins with "The effect," it's the penultimate passage in the second sentence: "The effect of SDA moves to consolidate power against opponents in Bihac, Tuzla and even in Sarajevo [In English] such as by purges of non-Muslim and independent Muslims from official positions, also means ever less restraint on the Bosnian Army's non-compliance with the cessation of hostilities agreement and on the government's media and diplomatic campaign against UNPROFOR." [Interpretation] So, Mr. Banbury, is it clear that the Muslim side violated all cease-fire agreements to our detriment and even to the detriment of the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Bosnian government side was often in non-compliance with various agreements including, in this case, the cease-fire agreement. I'm not aware of a single agreement in Bosnia during the UNPROFOR time that was ever fully respected.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now please see 1D3429.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your statement you said that we closed down the airport because we simply wished to show who was the boss and who was controlling everything in Sarajevo; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think in my statement I referred to a quote by you where you had said, through a press outlet, that you had decided to shut down the Sarajevo airport to show the world who was in control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, we can agree about the first part, Mr. Banbury, but let's have a look at the second part as well. Let's see what I noted as the reasons.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have page 4 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Paragraph (c): [In English] "Dr. Karadzic has passed on communique through BH civil affairs that BSA intend closing airport crossings for civilian traffic. Reasons given as continued smuggling of arms by BiH, continued sniping by BiH, BiH refusal to implement prisoner of war exchange, and BiH failure to honour cessation of hostilities." [Interpretation] These were the reasons, Mr. Banbury, rather than just showing that we were the ones who ruled. Were these the precise reasons as noted here?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe this passage refers to the so-called blue routes that used airport territory.
