This passage does not refer to closing the airport for flights but, rather, the blue routes that allowed civilians to pass from one territory to the other or from one side of Bosnian-controlled territory to the other through the airport. And these are the reasons you stated at the time for closing of those blue routes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1160, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please have 1D3427.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a document --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the accused please repeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the interpreters didn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I wanted to identify the document, that it's dated the 11th of July, Viktor Andreev is writing to Sergio Vieira de Mello and it was drafted by Tony Banbury. Do we agree about this?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us have page 4, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Paragraphs 10 and 11: [In English] "The utilities situation in the city continues to improve, with an emphasis being placed on water-supply due to the hot water. There is enough electricity being produced to meet the needs of the entire city, but cut-offs still occur for as of yet inexplicable and apparently non-technical reasons. "Sniping remains the greatest danger in Sarajevo, with lives of innocent civilians still being lost on both sides of the confrontation line on a regular basis to this insidious menace."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] "Prices in Sarajevo markets remain low due to steady access of commercial convoys to the city. Use of blue routes also remain high." [Interpretation] Mr. Banbury, was it clear to you that all these commercial goods could only get in via Serb-held territory and that both commercial goods and humanitarian aid arrived in at least 80 per cent of the quantities that had originally been envisaged?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- the movement of commercial goods in and out of Sarajevo and indeed humanitarian goods varied according to different times in the war. Sometimes access was relatively good, sometimes it was not. At this point in time with the blue routes open, commercial goods were being allowed to transit the blue routes with agreement of the Bosnian Serb authorities, and those commercial goods, as indicated on paragraph 13, had a positive impact on the situation in the city. It's also the case that humanitarian goods were able to move in and out of the city at this time with a positive impact. It was not always that way, but at this point in time, in the week of 3 to 9 July 1994, that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is what I'm putting to you, Mr. Banbury, that even incidents that were frequent and violations of the cease-fire did not lead to impediments in terms of life in the city itself. The impediments were caused by the activity of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina from the city of Sarajevo. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The impediments to life in the city of Sarajevo with respect to humanitarian goods, commercial goods, risk to civilians were always caused by the Bosnian Serb authorities and Bosnian Serb military. The reasons why the Bosnian Serb authorities, the Bosnian military may have decided to cause those impediments and why they fluctuated from time to time, I'm sure those reasons varied and had a lot to with activities of the Bosnian government and the Bosnian military. Nonetheless, the impediments were caused by the Bosnian Serb authorities and Bosnian Serb military.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1161, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As regards 11, sniper activity: [In English] "Sniping remains the greatest danger in Sarajevo, with lives of innocent civilians still being lost on both sides of the confrontation line on a regular basis to this insidious menace." [Interpretation] Do you find this acceptable, from your document, that there were deaths on both sides of the front line due to sniping, as it was put here?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why did you write this? Oh, it must be a question of interpretation. No, do you understand that that was the case? I mean, of course that you do not say that that was so, but do you accept that this is what the report says?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what the report says and that was happening at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In one paragraph you say that Mladic confirmed -- in response to the question as to why snipers were active in Sarajevo again, he said that it was because somewhere the Muslims were not observing their cease-fire. But then comes your interpretation, that Mladic admitted that his snipers were firing at civilians. However, that is not what his statement says. And now could we briefly look at P1208. While we are waiting for it, Mr. Banbury, do you agree that sniper activity is legal? This is paragraph 94. That was paragraph 94 of your statement where you speak about that. 94 and 95. You thought that Mladic explicitly: [In English] "... explicit recognition by Mladic of BSA responsibility for sniping is somewhat surprising." In 95 you say: [In English] "... they are admitting to use sniping civilians as a punitive measure rather than for military gains." [Interpretation] The problem does not lie in the document, the problem lies in the interpretation. Can you indicate where it was that Mladic admitted that, that there was sniper activity against civilians?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: You, I think, asked me two questions. One was whether sniper activity is legal. I am not an expert on the Laws of War, but I believe in a military-to-military context it is, but I'm not sure. I am fairly certain that sniping activity against civilians is illegal. With respect to where Mladic admitted that there was sniper activity against civilians, in the passage that you referred to where he acknowledged sniping by his forces in the Sarajevo area, it was, in my understanding, a reference to sniping against civilians because it was always in the context of civilian casualties that we were raising sniping with the Bosnian government as well as the Bosnian Serbs. We did not, according to my recollection, really express concern or get involved or object when it was military-on-military sniping. Maybe we may have mentioned it as an issue on a rare occasion, but it was never -- I don't recall ever having done so, it wasn't a priority. Sniping against civilians was very high priority for us. We were working in many different ways to try and limit it and protect civilians, and as the earlier weekly report says, there were civilian deaths on both sides. So it was clear that the Bosnian Serbs were targeting civilians in their sniping and that was our big concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That cannot be proven, Mr. Banbury. Those are opinions. An example of a lack of understanding is paragraph 94, where there's a reference to Mladic, and also 95. By way of interpretation you are altering what actually happened to civilians. Look at this order of the 30th of June, 1994. Paragraph 3 says, in the strictest possible terms, enemy targets, (officers and soldiers) enemy personnel. So it's officers and soldiers, and that is what Mladic could have admitted, that there was intensified activities, sniper activity, and he did not accept and he did not mention nor would he allow that to be used against civilians. Isn't that right? In paragraph 94 there is no admission to that, that it pertains to civilians?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- the fact of Bosnian Serb military targeting innocent civilians in Sarajevo through snipers is extremely well established. I have no idea how many victims of sniping there were, innocent civilians, but there were many, and it was an issue that we worked hard on. We constantly raised it to the attention of yourself, of General Mladic, of other senior Bosnian Serb authorities. There's no question that Bosnian Serb military targeted civilians through sniping in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you believe that any gun-fire is sniper fire aimed at civilians?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you accept that every one of these assertions with regard to intentional targeting of civilians calls for an investigation to establish who it was that did the firing, whether it was stray bullets or whether it was intentional targeting of civilians? Do you agree that that has to be established by way of an investigation?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: UNPROFOR routinely investigated sniping incidents and sought to determine to the best of our ability the -- or we routinely investigated civilian deaths in Sarajevo caused by gun-fire and sought to establish to the best of our ability the source of the gun-fire, in other words, the direction and whether this was sniping or random gun-fire. The normal personal weapon of soldiers in the Bosnian conflict had certain type of calibre bullets. There wasn't only one weapon but it was the bullets were of a certain calibre. Sniping bullets are of a different calibre, different nature, and as I understand it, though I'm not an expert, cause different kinds of wounds, and so it was normally possible for UNPROFOR investigators to determine whether the -- there was a -- whether the death was caused by sniper fire or was random gun-fire. And I know for a fact that we were able to establish on many occasions that civilian casualties caused by gun-fire were caused by direct sniper fire. And by the way, it wasn't just civilian casualties, there were UNPROFOR soldiers killed by sniper fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say -- actually, please, for the sake of time, I will really have to ask you to stay tomorrow as well because there are so many subjects that we haven't even touched upon. Are you trying to say that more civilians were killed by sniper fire than by stray bullets, random gun-fire?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry if my response was confusing. I am not trying to say that. I'm trying to -- I'm saying that UNPROFOR was able to establish in many cases in Sarajevo that civilians were killed by sniper fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you give the OTP those findings, they would appreciate it highly. These findings where it was established beyond any doubt that it was the Serbs that did the firing. That would be very good and very useful because that would actually refute your assertions. And I have to struggle against them because they are just sweeping statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, unnecessary comments on your part. It's argumentative. Come to your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we then please have D827.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at this, what General van Baal is writing to Jovan Divjak on the 13th of August and the 15th of August. First we are going to deal with the 13th of August --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us wait until we have the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please focus on this, on the 13th of August, General van Baal is writing to General Divjak, and he is saying what led to the closing of the airport and to delays in flights and closing the UNHCR air-lift. And it says: "Even though you have given assurances to this command of free and unimpeded use of the airport, it again turned out that these three bullets fired from territory held by the RBiH Army resulted in the suspension of air-lifts which are used to provide food to people. In essence, this was an irrational act." And so on and so forth. Can we now have D828. Were those the reasons for the cancellation of the air-lift and is it the fault of the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular incident, the closure of the airport was the result of gun-fire coming from territory controlled by the Bosnian government authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Take a look at what General van Baal is writing on the 15th, again to General Divjak of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. "Today, on and 15th of August, 1994, at approximately 1100 hours, a UN aircraft was hit by a single small arms round," and so on and so forth. Then it says your representative officially condemned this practice of targeting aircraft. And then it says: "I'm counting on your full co-operation in the near future to ban these terrorist activities on UN aircraft which are bringing in food for the people of Bosnia-Herzegovina." This happened only two days later from the same place and at the same time. Is this yet another incident for -- which was not the fault of the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to see the full UNPROFOR report on this incident, but based on this letter, I, in principle, would agree that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D3433, can we have that, please. 1D3433.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 14th of September, 1994. Could you please focus on this. It is Koljevic and Muratovic that are meeting and it was facilitated by Mr. Andreev. And he prosed this agenda, he left them to work on this on their own, and then he returned to see what they had achieved.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have a look at the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: To read it in English: [In English] "On the subject of sniping, they noted with satisfaction the recent reduction of the incidents of sniping. Seeking to build on this foundation, they agreed to explore the possibility of an extended agreement which would include all small calibre weapons. (General Soubirou notes that more Sarajevo civilians are killed by stray bullets from the active front line than are killed by snipers)." "There was no detailed discussion on the routes around Sarajevo, though they did endorse my proposal that the re-opening of the routes be done in three phases: Movement for civilians, movement for humanitarian goods, movement for commercial goods." [Interpretation] Do you know that this meeting was facilitated by Mr. Andreev and do you accept what General Soubirou says, namely, that the front line was nearby and that stray bullets are killing more people than snipers?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree that this meeting was facilitated by Mr. Andreev. With regard to General Soubirou's observation, I think it needs to be clarified whether he was referring to the entire course of the war, that period right then. I'm not exactly sure what he meant by that, and I think UNPROFOR documentation in terms of investigating civilian deaths, et cetera, would provide greater clarity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1162, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have 1D3446.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we are waiting for it, do you remember that in one of these documents you noted down and informed me that an UNPROFOR convoy was disturbed at the Dobrun check-point by the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't recall that specific incident. I'm sure it's just my memory. If there's documentation or more information about it, I would probably recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, we have it in one of the documents that we tendered. However, look at my reaction. This is a document whereby the Drina Corps -- or, rather, it is being sent by the Main Staff to the commander of the Drina Corps and it says: [In English] "The president of the Republika Srpska has informed us in writing of incidents of improper and unprofessional conduct by personnel manning check-points towards personnel and convoys of the UNHCR as follows:" [Interpretation] And now you can see this for yourself, I don't have to read it out. You will see what the information provided to me was, how they were disturbed, as it were.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is also strictly confidential, so it was not meant for the media. [In English] "The president of the Republika Srpska issued a warning to the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska Army over the improper and unprofessional conduct of the personnel at the Dobrun check-point and requested a detailed investigation of the above-mentioned incidents and requested a list of names at the check-point personnel that inspected the UNPROFOR [sic] on 14th, 16th, 20th and 21st of August, 1994. He also wants to know where the items taken from the convoys are now, on whose orders the convoys' cargo was taken and what measures were taken against those who are responsible for the incidents. "The president of Republika Srpska ordered the Main Staff and Drina Corps command to train the personnel at the check-point in Dobrun and audit their work while inspecting UNHCR convoys announced for 23 and 25 of August." [Interpretation] Do you agree that the president of the republic cannot do more than this?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So what is it that the president of the republic can do except for issuing an order to have procedure observed?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The problem of UNHCR convoys or UNPROFOR convoys -- as was also mentioned in that document where the Russians were turned back because the convoy had mattresses and kitchen utensils, these problems persisted throughout the war and the Bosnian Serb authorities, civilian and military, had a responsibility to ensure such problems did not exist and the means by which they were to fulfill that obligation is something that was really up to them. For UNPROFOR, for me, what mattered was whether the obligations were fulfilled or not. They were not. They were constantly raised -- the concerns were constantly raised with you, with General Mladic, with other senior Serb officials and we were never satisfied with the actions on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The first question, I'm going to try to deal with this on a yes-or-no basis for the sake of time, do you think that the question of military convoys should be resolved by civilian authorities or should it be resolved by the military? How can civilian authorities control the military, your military, as it were? It is your military convoys that I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military in principle should operate under overall civilian control. It's the highest civilian authorities that should provide direction to the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This order of the president of the republic, is that not exactly what you've been saying now? It's an order for the military to correct a mistake?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that order is helpful or in principle ought to have been helpful. The order ought to have been followed up and when the practice wasn't adhered to, disciplinary action should have been taken against the chain of command. Further, the whole premise of the check-points and inspections and everything was one that ought not to have been instituted in the manner it was. So, a very different policy, in my view, ought to have been followed by the Bosnian Serb authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, we can conclude from your answer that either this was respected or the chain of command was disrupted; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The policy, from my perspective, needs to be looked at over the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I am sorry, I'm speaking about this order. I'm talking about this order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please don't interrupt the witness when answering. Yes, Mr. Banbury, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. There were times when the Bosnian Serb authorities let our convoys through, and certainly we were glad that that happened in those circumstances. There were many, many, many, many other times when we had problems with UNPROFOR convoys, UNHCR convoys. The issue of freedom of movement and convoys, from my view, needs to be looked at over the course of the conflict, and we had very significant problems with our convoys. We had military fuel trucks stolen, we had military jeeps stolen, we had weapons stolen, we had supplies stolen, all from the Bosnian Serb military authorities. That had significant military significance. The supplies that were taken from UNPROFOR military by the Bosnian Serbs aided the Serb war effort. So while this order is helpful, the policy implemented on the ground over the sustained period of time that I was in Bosnia was extremely unhelpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we admit this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, I take it you don't have a opposition to the admission of this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In relation to this document, what was your -- I didn't follow what your question was. Either this was respected or the chain of command was disrupted. What did you mean? You put the question again to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This relies on the question what are the options of the president of the republic. If he issues an order, that order is either executed, or if it's not executed, then there is no change [as interpreted] of command. So I was asking Mr. Banbury if we had these two alternatives. It's one or the other, we can't have both.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree? The president of the republic can issue an order, can monitor its execution, its executed, so there is a chain of command, or it's not executed and there is no chain of command?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that the president can issue an order and it should be respected, and if it's not, then it should be -- or the implementation of the order should be monitored. I don't know whether this -- the implementation of this was monitored. I don't know whether follow-up action was taken in incidents where there were -- there was not respect for the conditions in the order. I do know that we did not have the freedom of movement and the conditions we wanted, whether it's at check-points or movement of our convoys.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This will be admitted as Exhibit D1163.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at your paragraph 56 in your statement of the 1st of September, 1994: "Karadzic said at the Assembly session that the Contact Group plan is dead and that he says, in English, I'm going to read it: [In English] "We will impose sanctions against Muslims so toughly that a bird could not pass through. A rough English version of the Radovan Karadzic speech, Dr. Karadzic speech was transmitted to our office, copy," and so on. [Interpretation] Please now look at paragraph 58 of the 3rd of September: [In English] "Karadzic was quoted as saying: In the event an arms embargo was lifted, the Serbs would take UN blue helmets hostage, shoot down a lot of planes and arrest all foreigners." [Interpretation] Are these two statements contained in the two cited paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at D703 so that we can see exactly what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is my letter to Mr. Akashi: [In English] "Excellency, thank you for your letter of 3rd of September. Extracts from my speech, to which you refer, have been reported out of context. We do not, at present, intend to impose any sanctions against the Muslims. A decision to introduce such sanctions, moreover, would not affect normal humanitarian aid provided that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia is not blocking humanitarian aid destined to Republika Srpska." [Interpretation] Then it goes on to say: [In English] "Since Yugoslavia is imposing economic sanctions against us, we feel entitled to continue commercial sanctions against the Muslims. As you know, however, this policy does not cover gas, water, and electricity supplies to the Muslims. You are, of course, aware that the Muslim leadership in Sarajevo is openly delighted at the recent turn of events in the relations between Yugoslavia and the Republika Srpska," and so on. [Interpretation] Did you know that Yugoslavia was preventing, completely preventing commercial traffic towards Republika Srpska but also all humanitarian traffic towards the Drina? It wasn't completely preventing it, but it was making it more difficult, and that our threats at the address of the Muslims only had to do with the commercial traffic?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware that there were significant restrictions placed on the movement of commercial goods from the FRY, Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, to the Bosnian Serb-controlled area. With respect to your second question, that threats at the address of the Muslims only had to do with the commercial traffic, I think the statements are unclear with that regard, the quote that I have from the speech. In addition, the letter you addressed to Mr. Akashi links humanitarian assistance to Muslims to whether or not Yugoslavia is letting humanitarian assistance pass through to you. That is seriously objectionable. No humanitarian organisation or the United Nations could ever accept that provision of humanitarian assistance to a civilian population in need could be dependent upon behaviour of another group and access to another area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this is an appeal to Mr. Akashi to exert pressure on Yugoslavia to stop disrupting our humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I do not read it as an appeal to Mr. Akashi to approach the Yugoslav authorities on this issue. That being said, I'm quite certain that in instances where the Yugoslav authorities were placing limits on the delivery of humanitarian assistance through their territory to the Bosnian Serbs, UNPROFOR would have raised that concern and insisted that humanitarian assistance be allowed to pass freely through Yugoslavia to the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 1D3434, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is the 15th of September, 1994. Dejan Mihov sending a message to Viktor Andreev. The whole text is very interesting but we don't have time. Can we have page 3, please. Ten days after my letter to Ambassador Akashi, this is what the humanitarian situation looks like: [In English] "... with a good week for the air-lift, 83 flights and two land convoys, the food situation in the city is good. UNHCR transported 1300 metric tonnes of food aid. Due to the fact that 100 per cent of the food needs are met, UNHCR and WFP will activate a stockpile project for food for the winter, which will allow the agency to have four weeks' reserve to be used in case of emergency." [Interpretation] Do you agree that my warnings and threats did not result in any shortages or reductions and that the situation is actually satisfactory?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The passage cited refers to Sarajevo and the -- Mr. Mihov was in charge of Sector Sarajevo. I agree that in that area at that time the delivery of humanitarian supplies was satisfactory.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1164, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 1D3462.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the same day that Mr. Mihov is reporting about in this previous document, this is what General Brinkman writes to General Delic, the commander of the Muslim Army: "Dear General, on the 15th of September, 1994, two humanitarian convoys were approved to travel between Visoko and Sarajevo as agreed by both warring parties." And so on. And then the next sentence states: "This morning between 1055 and 1105 hours, the second convoy destined for the city of Sarajevo warehouses (the first convoy was destined for Rajlovac)" in the Serbian territory. This is not in the text, I am explaining this to you, you know where Rajlovac is. "As it was stationary, the UNPROFOR check-point Papa Cekrcici, 3 kilometres east of Visoko, was engaged by five rounds of 60-millimetre mortar from a B and H baseplate. Miraculously, there were no injuries." And then the details are given. "There was no BSA provocation nor were there any BSA in the immediate area for the mortar to be targeting. This was a direct and deliberate attack against UNPROFOR. This was the first humanitarian convoy to use this route for several months and was meant to represent the opening of the route for this purpose." And so on. Can you see, Mr. Banbury, that the Muslim side is disrupting the road to Visoko that we opened, it was disrupting the road for some reason and it fired five mortars?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall the specific incident. I accept that it occurred as described in the letter of General Brinkman. We did at times have obstructions imposed upon us by Bosnian government authorities. They were relatively few, relatively limited and relatively easy to solve and did not constitute a broad-spread practice of stopping our humanitarian assistance convoys.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1165, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 120 of your statement, you speak about the killing of two French soldiers that were erecting anti-sniping barricades in Snipers Alley. Who killed the first of the victims?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the documentation I reviewed on that subject, the -- the source of that attack was not able to be determined by UNPROFOR. We don't know who killed them. We don't know where that came from, which side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does this also apply to the second one?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In the second case, we were able to establish that the source of the fire was from Bosnian Serb-controlled territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The Defence asserts that the first one was killed by the Muslim side and that the UNPROFOR did state its position on that, and in the second case, it was not possible to establish that even though it was made to look as if it came from the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreters did not get the number of the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat the number again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D3450.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 16th of April, 1995. It's a United Nations document. This is Michael Moussalli and then already Enrique Aguilar instead of the previous person, and at the bottom it states: [In English] "The two French soldiers killed by sniper fire in as many days ... the deliberate targeting of the UNPROFOR soldiers could have an implication for French participants," and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It states here that one of the them was killed in Dobrinja on the 14th of April, and on the 15th of April: [In English] "Another French soldier was killed by sniping, this time while erecting an anti-sniping barricade on Sniper Alley. Investigation of the first incident has so far proven inconclusive and it is unlikely that evidence will be sufficient to attribute responsibility for the murder. Initial investigation into the second death indicates that the firing came from a building well within the Bosnian Serb-controlled territory, at which a French anti-sniping post returned fire immediately after the incident. The final conclusion of the investigation has, however, not been reached." [Interpretation] So the final results of the investigation did not describe that to the Serbs, is this what the document states?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it said the final conclusion had not yet been reached. The investigation -- investigations of this nature were conducted very thoroughly by UNPROFOR. There were preliminary conclusions based on the fact the firing had come from a building well within Serb-controlled territory, at which the French anti-sniping team returned fire. So we had our preliminary conclusions with which we had some confidence the investigation was going to be completed. I don't know the results, the final results of that investigation. I have no information to indicate that they are anything different than the initial results, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I know that you are not a lawyer, but do you agree that if it was not established, then it cannot be ascribed to either side; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think it's a question for the witness to answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It already is, as a Prosecution exhibit, as part of the associated exhibits for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I draw your attention to paragraph 128 of your statement. Where you talk about -- this is in the second half of the paragraph where you say: [In English] "Gvero said that in the Srebrenica enclave, the Muslim military commander has tens of tonnes of fuel which he got from the convoys entering Srebrenica. He affirmed that they would not allow the enemy to build stocks of food and fuel under the guise of humanitarian aid. Smith said that there was no evidence whatsoever that the Dutch or British had been giving fuel away, and Gvero laughed. Smith asked for evidence as to how the fuel was being sold or given away and Gvero said he would provide this information at a later meeting." [Interpretation] Did you attend this meeting?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I did. I'd have to confirm that, but I believe, yes, I was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is what Gvero said correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have D1029 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, could you give the exhibit number of the previous document for the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It hasn't been assigned as yet, Your Honour, because there were a number of associated exhibits, but it was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you give us the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's been assigned as Exhibit P2486.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at this report by the Birac Brigade of the 12th of May, 1995. Paragraph 4. At the top it states fuel is being smuggled in double -- this is an order, is being smuggled. And then in 4 it states: "Confiscate the surplus of fuel from large tanks leaving just the quantity needed for their journey to the enclave and back to the check-point. On their return from the enclave, return the fuel against a receipt note for quantities confiscated and/or returned."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Before that the accused said: They smuggled fuel in double or large tanks on combat and non-combat vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So does this indicate that Gvero had a foundation for his assertions, and he got this report from Colonel Andric in this dispatch, so did Colonel Gvero have enough grounds to make this particular assertion?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Gvero asserts that in Zepa there were ten tonnes of fuel held by the Bosnian government authorities that had been taken from or -- taken from UNPROFOR or given by UNPROFOR. I do not believe there are any grounds for having made that assertion. I'm unaware of any cases where the UNPROFOR was handing over fuel to the Bosnian military, and I certainly do not believe that UNPROFOR willingly or against its will provided ten tonnes of fuel to the Bosnian government forces in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: After the break, Mr. Banbury, we will show you a Muslim document which indicates that, and it's not talking about tens -- scores of tonnes but hundreds of thousands of tonnes. But before that we are going to look at document 1D3460.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D3460.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You recognise this document; is that right? This is already Aguilar on duty.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We can see here that UNPROFOR is aware that -- you can see that an offensive is being prepared. And then it goes on to say: [In English] "Adding to fear over the future escalation of the conflict in Bihac, where the BH troops re-organisation and training activities throughout central Bosnia in preparation for a spring offensive. Aircraft sightings over Bosnia were suspected to be part of an effort to reinforce military units during the delivery of equipment and money." [Interpretation] Is Carter's -- so-called Carter's truce in force or in effect at that time? This is the 18th of February.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the four-month cessation of hostilities agreement was in principle in force at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you look at what it says about Sarajevo: [In English] "Sarajevo is experiencing one of the best times since the start of the war. The blue routes are open, with more than 5.000 people using the routes daily. Availability of gas, water, and electricity has greatly improved, and there are very few incidents of cease-fire violations and firing incidents. Although, BH forces occasionally try to enter the demilitarised zone, the Mount Igman area is generally quiet." [Interpretation] Mr. Banbury, can this be done without the Serbs respecting the cease-fire, and is the Serb contribution here to the improvement of the situation in Sarajevo clear and indisputable?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe the Serb contribution to the improvement of the situation in Sarajevo at this time is clear.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we admit this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1166, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, it's time to have our second break, after which you will have 40 minutes to conclude your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask you to review this again. We are going to leave many topics untouched, and in particular each statement would need to be -- the comments in the statements would need to be clarified. I think we asked for 30 hours for this witness and we got 20 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just for planning purposes, how long would you need for your re-examination, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Keeping in mind that the cross hasn't been concluded, right now I'd say 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll have a break for half an hour and resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you'll have additional half an hour, which means you'll have to conclude your cross-examination by ten past 2.00, which also means the Prosecution will have 20 minutes for its re-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now please see 65 ter 22794.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: A little while ago, Mr. Banbury, I promised you a document from the Ministry of Internal Affairs of the state security service of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We also have a translation of this document so I would kindly ask if we could show that one as well. It's their document, and as we have no time, can we please move to --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, yes, can we please move to page 7 in the English version and page 6 in the Serbian version of this document. It says here that from humanitarian aid -- in Serbian version we need page 6, rather than page 5, which we can see now, and in English version page 7. The following page in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And around the middle of the page, from humanitarian page many goods were taken aside for the needs of the 28th Division, of which considerable part for Oric were sent at the market by Hamdija Fejzic, Suljo Konakovic, Amir Mehmedovic, and so on. And further down, item 2, Suljo Hasanovic, former chief of the People's Defence Secretariat, according some information Hasanovic took foods and food items from the depot of the -- for the humanitarian aid. This is on page 8 in the English version. And he used to sell some of that on the market with the help of unknown persons and so on and so forth. Suljo Hasanovic. Item 2 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please see page 9 in the English version, and page 8 in the Serbian version. No, rather, page 7 in the Serbian version. The following page in Serbian, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Item 5: "Dr. Avdo Hasanovic, chief of the war hospital in Srebrenica, medicines from the hospital supplies were sold at 100 to 200 German marks, which caused a large number of deaths, mostly among the ARBiH troops."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And if we could please turn the page in the Serbian text, and in English it's fine. Number 6 at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is information that Stitkovac was buying oil in Zepa and selling it in Srebrenica. We can turn the page. Item number 6, Stitkovac buying it from the Ukrainian Battalion and selling it in Srebrenica. This is a document from the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is to say, the Muslim one. So, Mr. Banbury, do you see that you were not aware of everything that was going on in the enclaves and that General Gvero, as it seems, knew that better than yourself?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have previously acknowledged that I did not know nor did I ever suggest I knew everything that was going on in the enclaves. I do have a lot of experience in humanitarian situations on the Thai-Cambodian border and with the World Food Programme and there -- it is impossible for humanitarian organisations to prevent food from going or humanitarian assistance from going to sources other than its original intention. Some of that is perfectly legitimate. If we give food, dry rations, rice, whatever, beans, to a family and they decide to sell some on the market in order to purchase vegetables or medicine, that's routine and always happens. There's also almost always some misappropriation of humanitarian assistance, whether it's in a place like Somalia where it's very high or other cases where it's very low, it always happens. As for the fuel here, I certainly do not rule out the possibility that the Ukrainian Battalion sold for their own profit some fuel to whoever those people were. Sadly, that, too, happens at times in large peacekeeping operations. I am unaware of that being a very prevalent issue in the safe areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, Mr. Banbury, this does not have do with families selling this at the market, but, rather, state officials. The authorities in Srebrenica are abusing the storage and selling humanitarian goods which we allowed to pass through our territory. And please have a look at this as well, they are also dealing in rifles and ammunition and fuel, which was not brought by UNHCR for certain. They somehow obtained it in some other way. So would you agree that this was an abuse of the storage or the depot rather than that it was a family who gave them that, or a family who put it out on the market?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not rule out the possibility that some of the local authorities in the safe areas in Eastern Bosnia misappropriated humanitarian assistance from warehouses. That is possible.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, it's very difficult to see a basis upon which we can admit this document through this witness. Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I don't see any whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is directly connected with the reasons for imposing restrictions on the sorts of materiel that would be allowed to enter the enclaves. Our army had information that there was trafficking in arms, ammunition, and oil, and believed that such quantities should not enter the enclaves because that was eventually turned against us. Because it wasn't just the civilian population that was there. The enclaves were not demilitarised and it was the army that -- who used the food, used the oil, and there was the smuggling of weapons and so on, if you have a look at item 9 which is on the screen right now. So would you agree that this is the area --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you did put your question to the witness based upon this document. The witness was not able to give proper foundation upon which we can admit this document, as was the case with General Smith, we'll not admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But he allowed for the possibility that there was abuse and that he was not aware of everything that was going on in the enclaves, and in my view, this is the basis for admitting the document. I believe it should be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, we have given our ruling. Please move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now see 1D3365, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a telegram from Mr. Annan to Mr. Akashi. Please have a look at it. It's the air supply for eastern enclaves from Sarajevo. And then it says in paragraph 2: [In English] "We would grateful if you would provide a comprehensive assessment of the actual supply situation in the safe areas both for UNPROFOR and UNHCR. According to your daily sitreps, UNPROFOR continues to have access by land convoys (although we note the absence of fuel deliveries in recent days). Preliminary information obtained from UNHCR likewise seems to indicate that humanitarian supplies, in principle, do not appear to be running low - we hear they are currently meeting 75 per cent of their targets." [Interpretation] I said a little while ago up to 80 per cent. Would you agree that Mr. Annan and Mr. Akashi agreed, on the basis of reports, that 75 per cent of the objectives, that is to say, the needs of the humanitarian assistance which was envisaged, were indeed reached?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The cable here from Mr. Annan is referring to other reporting. I'm not exactly sure what reporting that is. It does indicate that their report suggests 75 per cent of the UNHCR targets for the eastern enclaves were being met at that particular time. I know from my humanitarian background that any time we are falling short of humanitarian assistance targets, it poses a very serious problem for the beneficiary population because the 100 per cent target is to meet the bare-minimum requirements. Humanitarian agencies don't provide excess food to people, they provide the bare minimum necessary for a healthy diet, a non -- kind of -- to give them enough nutrition. So anything short of that presents a serious problem. I also note that the fact that UNPROFOR was recommending aerial resupply of the enclaves was a very serious -- indicated a very serious situation that reflected, one, the restrictions in -- the regular routine pattern of restrictions imposed upon us by the Bosnian Serb authorities, and, two, the dire situation that had finally been reached in the enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Banbury, if the Srebrenica population was 45.000, as reported to you, then perhaps it would be 75 per cent, but if the population was 35.000 to 37.000, as the Muslim documents show, then it would be sufficient; correct? Would you agree that if the population was smaller than represented, then it would constitute more than 75 per cent?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree that if the actual civilian population in, in this case, Srebrenica was smaller than the target population for UNHCR and if the UNHCR stock was 75 per cent for its target population, then the actual per cent of humanitarian assistance available would be higher. That's a mathematical calculation, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can it be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1167, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 1D3376.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As early as on the 6th of July, 1995, you were at the headquarters in Zagreb with Mr. Akashi; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here is a document which was sent by Mr. Corwin to Mr. Akashi on the 6th of July. I just wish to point the first paragraph to you: [In English] "I had long talk with Professor Koljevic this afternoon in Pale. He said that President Karadzic was very eager to meet with Carl Bildt. The Serbs considered that the situation was deteriorating especially with regard to humanitarian aid and they wanted to meet urgently."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we turn the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here, item 6 and second sentence: [In English] "... several times that he was concerned about the deteriorating humanitarian situation." [Interpretation] Last sentence: In item 7 he expresses, he says that we are not happy about the course that the army might follow considering the situation that we are in. Have you been in a position to see or were you aware about Mr. Corwin meeting Professor Koljevic, and would you accept that Professor Koljevic expressed our concern about the deterioration of the humanitarian situation?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Mr. Corwin did, as part of his responsibilities, at times meet with Professor Koljevic, and I accept that Professor Koljevic, in this particular reference meeting, voiced an expression of concern regarding the deteriorating humanitarian situation. I also note, as clearly reflected in paragraph 7, that there may have been different motivations for that expression and it is not my experience that the -- that during my period in Bosnia, the Bosnian Serb authorities ever showed a genuine concern for the humanitarian situation of non-Serbs, but instead responded to that situation based on consideration of a wide range of factors and their own assessment of their own interests, and in this case, perhaps an interest that was developing as a result of a changing strategic situation in Sarajevo and in Bosnia in April 1995. Or July 1995, excuse me, in this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Banbury, if we had more time, I would try to refute your statement that we didn't need to do many things but we did them anyway. But I see this statement of yours as anti-Serbian; is that correct or not? How can you say that the Serbs didn't do anything that they didn't have to and that they didn't take care about others? What is the basis for such a statement? Do you have any evidence?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't feel I was ever anti any party or pro any party to the conflict. I was pro-UNPROFOR and pro-civilian population. And in my experience in Bosnia, civilian populations on all sides suffered, and the attitude or the behaviour of the Bosnian Serb authorities toward the humanitarian plight of the non-Serb population was reprehensible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You are used to this, Mr. Banbury, because you heard it from Muslim propaganda, isn't that right? It is identical to what the Muslim propaganda was saying. What you are mentioning now is your conclusions. I have no objections to what you wrote. What I'm interested in is why your interpretation of your documents are so drastically different from the documents themselves?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is that a question, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Why is the interpretation -- I'm asking Mr. Banbury this: Your documents are self-explanatory. They are self-explanatory, so why is your interpretation poorer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Come to specific issues instead of making arguments.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm just responding generally to general statements. Could we now see 1D3371, please. And can the previous document be admitted. I thought it has already been admitted. The witness confirmed that he is aware of these meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1168, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, please focus your attention on this. It's another document from Phillip Corwin to Mr. Akashi. The date is 17th of July. And item 1 says that the Bosnian minister, Hasan Muratovic demanded that he leave Bosnia immediately. And he says, "I see this intimidation as part of a campaign," and so on and so forth. [In English] "... to render inoperative the civilian components of the UNPROFOR. The Bosnian government and the BSA as well are not interested in peace talks. They are both interested in military solution. I also think it is a serious matter when the government minister from a member state of the United Nations threatens the life of the United Nations official." [Interpretation] And we can see everything else that's there. Were you aware of such intimidation and do you believe that the United Nations representatives were allowed to criticise the Muslim side openly, to talk openly considering such intimidations?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: UNPROFOR officials, from the Special Representative of the Secretary-General on down, routinely criticised the Bosnian government civilian and military authorities for a whole range of issues throughout the war. I think the historical records speaks to that quite clearly. In the case of Mr. Corwin, and I'm familiar with this case, Mr. Corwin did not have the confidence of many of his colleagues in UNPROFOR. He was not reliable and he was one of the few and perhaps the only person who was ever made persona non-grata from UNPROFOR by the Bosnian Serb authorities. I think this reflects more on Mr. Corwin than on anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Banbury, is there a single Frenchman who is good, in your opinion? Oh, he is American. I thought he was French, because today you disqualified the French generals. Is there anyone who is good enough, Mr. Banbury?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, that's a -- frankly, a ridiculous question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I withdraw the question. Can this document be admitted, please, because Mr. Banbury is aware of the intimidations mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1169, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And I say, the Defence says, Mr. Banbury, that Mr. Corwin is notorious among the Muslims because he talked publicly about the abuse that they carried out.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now could we now please have D1127 to see why he was a persona non-grata.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before that, Mr. Banbury, would you like to comment on Mr. Karadzic's statement, Mr. Corwin is notorious among the Muslims because he talked about the abuse.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I think as I mentioned, it's a -- and it was established, I believe, earlier in the course of my testimony that UNPROFOR, as a regular basis, criticised the Bosnian government leaders, civilian and military, for actions they took which were incompatible with their obligations toward UNPROFOR or the civilian populations. The issue was not one of whether an UNPROFOR official was willing to be critical or not of any party. The issue was one of whether UNPROFOR officials conducted themselves in an impartial manner, a fair manner, an objective manner, and it was my view, and I know for a fact the view of several of my colleagues, that Mr. Corwin did not conduct himself in a manner befitting of an official of the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have no time to ask you whether this was the official position of Mr. Akashi, but please have a look at item 1, and item 3 as well: [In English] "At the very last minute the Bosnian side this afternoon rejected a proposal to restore utilities to Sarajevo. The Serbian side had agreed to the necessary technical arrangements, arranged by Mr. John Fawcett from the Office of Special Co-ordinator for Sarajevo. But the Bosnian side insisted on UNPROFOR control of Bacevo (Sarajevo's main water-pumping station, which is in Serb-controlled territory) as well as several gas supply points." [Interpretation] We can all read everything. But item 3: [In English] "It appears the Bosnian side did not want the utilities restored. There are several possible reasons: By keeping their own people in need, they hope to gain world sympathy. The press is on their side and one can expect CNN (Clearly Not Neutral) to show pictures of starving Bosnians." [Interpretation] You can see other reasons here, and item 4 says: [In English] "They had requested the meeting, and were clearly in favour of restoring utilities. Our guess is that the 100.000 citizens of Serbian Sarajevo are suffering badly and are quite annoyed with their blood(y) brothers in Pale." [Interpretation] Is it correct that Mr. Corwin is not sparing any of the sides you but that it was only the Muslim side that threatened him with death?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an internal UN communication not designed for public consumption. In it he expresses his speculation as to why the Bosnian government side may have taken a position or not. Suffice it to say that myself and colleagues of mine did not trust Mr. Corwin's judgement or his analysis of the situation and we would not have treated his views very seriously.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you think that his assessment is incorrect and an incorrect report that the Muslims are obstructing the re-establishment of the operation of utilities?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I accept that at the conclusion of this meeting, the Bosnian government did not agree to turn the utilities back on. Why they did not do so, I don't know, and I cannot, from my own perspective, trust the assessment in here by Mr. Corwin as to what transpired at that meeting and why one or the other party may have acted in a given way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you find his speculations to be unacceptable, although he attended that meeting; right?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not place value on Mr. Corwin's speculations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does that pertain to anybody's speculations?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there are many people whose judgement, assessment, analysis, and, indeed, speculation I would place much higher value on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D282, can we have that, please. Could I please have the English translation on the other side of the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is an order, an order of mine, dated the 11th of July, which tightens responsibility and discipline in terms of passage of humanitarian convoys. Please have a look at this so I don't have to read it out. Please look at paragraph 1 and paragraph 4: "Convoys shall be inspected by joint commissions, a mixed commission," and you see who is there, "between the entry point and the front line, no further inspection shall be made." Were you aware of that? Did you know that we were issuing such orders?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was unfamiliar with this particular order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that consistent with what we were putting to you as our position?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your position had more elements than it, but this order does not appear to me to be inconsistent with the convoy requirements that you placed upon us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1170, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I now please have 1D283.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we are waiting for that, Mr. Banbury, if you are objecting to the existence of inspections and controls in general, then I have to understand that as a difference in concepts because it was our understanding that we were entitled to that and that international documents gave us the right to do this. So this may be the source of a great deal of misunderstandings between us. Would you agree on that?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not and did not at the time to -- object to some type of regime through which the Bosnian Serb authorities could receive the necessary assurances from UNPROFOR or UNHCR with respect to the contents of our convoy. Some control regime would have been acceptable. My objection is that, one, there was a policy in place by the Bosnian Serb authorities to block our freedom of movement inconsistent with obligations under Security Council resolutions, and that in pursuit of that policy, a control regime was used that was very onerous on us and very effective in blocking our access to critical areas for resupply of our own troops as well as humanitarian assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We don't have time, Mr. Corwin [sic], to prove by way of documents that 75 per cent and even more than that just managed to get through. But please try to focus on this document, an order of the 30th of July, where an order is issued by Karadzic for the Ministry of Defence and of the Interior to enable the unobstructed movement of workers of the commission for refugees and humanitarian aid. Just have a look at that, and all state organs should comply with this. You see who the addressees are. Is that in line with our declared position that you were familiar with?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: This refers to workers of the commission for refugees and humanitarian aid. Which commission was that? Was that a mixed commission of Bosnian Serb and Bosnian government officials?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, no. This is the commissioner for refugees of Republika Srpska. We had a great many refugees and we had a commissioner for refugees because there were refugees of all faiths and ethnicities. Did you know that we had a lot of refugees in Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was well aware that there were many Bosnian Serb refugees in the territory controlled by the Bosnian Serb authorities.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can it be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What question did you put to the witness in relation to this document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whether this document was an illustration -- or rather, whether it was in line with what we had declared in public in our contacts with the UN. In relation to this question, that is, the question of humanitarian aid and the functioning of humanitarian organisations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I understand this order, it's an order from you, as president of the Bosnian Serb republic, to Bosnian Serb entities to grant Bosnian Serb officials the ability to move in your territory. That was normal practice. It comes as no surprise to me that Bosnian officials were able to move in Bosnian Serb-controlled territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But this refers to the UNHCR and the UNCP -- oh, sorry, sorry. I got a bit confused. Just a moment. Yes, this says that they cannot be mobilised into units without the consent of the commissioner and so on. So if you agree, it was necessary for me to issue this kind of warning that Serbian humanitarian issues should be allowed unobstructed movement. Is that understandable in view of the fact that there was a civil war going on?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure how to answer that question, Dr. Karadzic. I find it totally normal that if there was a civilian commission working on refugees and humanitarian aid, that a proper order would be given to the relevant authorities to allow that commission or its members to work, and that they ought not to be mobilised for other purposes. It was a policy decision, it's a policy decision that makes sense to me, and an order was given to implement it. I see this as very normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is my point, perhaps I wasn't clear enough: Even Serb humanitarian organisations, the Serb commission for refugees, needed my assistance and support. It wasn't only foreign organisations and UN organisations, but Serb ones as well. Do you agree that this document confirms that Serb humanitarian organisations could also run into problems, otherwise this document wouldn't have been issued in the first place; right?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see the situation as very different. For anyone to move about the territory of the controlled by the Bosnian Serb authorities, presumably they needed some type of pass or identification to move through check-points, without which they were perhaps subject to interrogation, detention, or whatever. So these authorities were granted permission to move about. If there was a persistent problem during the course of the war and these folks were not able to move about, that would be an analogous situation. The fact that a decision was taken on a policy matter and an instruction was given, I think is very different than the situation in which UNPROFOR found itself.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this being admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, let's move on to another topic. I find it difficult how relevant this document is and I don't think we have --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 1D284.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I thought that it was obvious that Serb humanitarian organisations also needed my protection because there was a civil war going on. Here is another order which says: "Take all measures at all locations to protect and provide security for personnel and vehicles of the UNHCR and UNHCP at their places of residence and during movement." Do you agree that we had publicly declared and every now and then we secretly issued orders aimed at protecting international organisations?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if that was standard practice. I see this order signed by you. I assume it's accurate and was written at the time. I note that it was dated 27 October 1995, at the tail end of a very significant military campaign conducted by NATO and by the Bosnian Army, the Bosnian Croat Army and Croatia itself, and this was just before the start of the Dayton peace talks, so the context on 27 October 1995 was very different than the context that existed for a large portion of the time that I was in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this one be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1171, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Banbury, we don't have time to deal with the crisis in August and September in respect of the NATO bombing Serb -- Serb positions were bombed by NATO and I cannot deal with the crisis in Bihac either. However, I quickly like to go through some documents that I believe you must be familiar with.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D3430, can I have that, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The 17th of August, 1994, from Akashi to Annan. You see the marked part here: [In English] "As can be seen from the proposed agendas of both sides, our basic approach has been that overall military stabilisation, including more military self-restraint on the part of BH side, was a prerequisite for bringing about improvement in specific matters such as re-opening of airport routes, the Tuzla airport, and the better movement of humanitarian convoys. We therefore called for greater co-operation from the BH side in the establishment of our OPs, the exchange of liaison officers, and interposing the UNPROFOR troops," and so on. [Interpretation] Do you agree, Mr. Banbury, that what is particularly being highlighted here is the fact that the Muslim Army should exercise restraint and that that is a prerequisite for the airport routes and everything else that has to do with humanitarian convoys?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, the statement is accurate but the reason its accurate is because the Bosnian Serb authorities controlled each of those issues; opening of the airport routes, opening of the Tuzla airport, better movement of humanitarian convoys. It was the Bosnian Serb authorities who were imposing limits or preventing all of those and the only way that we assessed we were going to get Bosnian Serb co-operation on those was if the Bosnian government side exercised restraint. So, yes, we wanted the Bosnian government side to exercise restraint that would hopefully then influence decisions on the Bosnian Serb side to open up the airport routes, Tuzla airport, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Banbury, the Serb side had the right to ask for peace and for observance of the cease-fire so that it could meet its obligations as well. Do you agree that the Serb side had the right to prevent humanitarian issues from giving an advantage to the other side, the enemy? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree the Bosnian Serb side had a right to request peace. No, I do not agree that there is any justification for linking access by civilian populations to humanitarian assistance, linking that to any political or military issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
