utterances.text: Mr. Banbury, my question is the following: Whether the Serb side was authorised to stop any action that had been abused by the other side in order to gain military advantage. Does international law give us that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't make a legal determination particularly with respect to a hypothetical proposition such as the one you just made. I do agree that the Bosnian Serb authorities had a legitimate interest in not having exploitation by their enemy in a way or steps taken by their enemy that would strengthen their military position relative to the Bosnian Serbs. I still do not agree that there's any justification at all to link provision of humanitarian assistance to a civilian population with any other political, military, or other matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at this, where it says that the army of the Bosnian Serbs had previously intended to close the routes following the Muslim offensive in Ozren but had been prevented by doing so by UNPROFOR persuasion.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The previous page, it says: "However, it was sometimes difficult [In English] to determine exactly who was responsible for the shooting of aircraft, and there was, for example, strong suspicion that the last two firing incidents had emanated from the Butmir side (BH area)." [Interpretation] Is this familiar? Actually, first of all, do you agree that there were lines that were so close that it was hard to determine from where fire was coming, and secondly, do you agree -- or, rather, does this sound familiar to you, that there were these suspicions that the firing had come from Butmir?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree that the lines of confrontation in the area of the Sarajevo airport sometimes made it hard to determine from where firing against the airport or UN aircraft occurred. Other times we were able to determine where the firing came from. I also agree that there were concerns that there was firing coming from both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When speaking of the Muslim side you always have to add the Serbian side at least a bit and that is why I'm so worried about your impartiality, Mr. Banbury.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to comment on that statement, Mr. Banbury?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I hope that the documents have shown that UNPROFOR was committed to establishing facts whenever we could and we let the facts and the reality of the situation on the ground determine our behaviour. The officials that I worked most closely with, did not have a -- and it's certainly the case for myself as well, did not have a political agenda, national agenda, a preference for any party. We were deeply concerned about peace, about the impact of the war on the civilian population. We spoke out against any party when they acted against their responsibilities or commitments. There were patterns of behaviour during the course of the war that I think speak for themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Banbury. That will be admitted as Exhibit D1172.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 1D3432. Again, September 1994. We can move on to page 7. It's General de Lapresle, he is sending this document to these addresses down here. And can we now have a look at page 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please look at B, yes. 13 UNHCR and one Red Cross flights landed at Sarajevo airport. So there were 14 flights on that day. [In English] "UNHCR-led convoys delivered a total of 1381 metric tonnes of humanitarian aid." It's on the next page. Do you agree, Mr. Banbury, that the average was over 8, 9, 10, 11 flights every day at Sarajevo airport when the airport was operating?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the airport was operating, there were a significant number of flights on a daily basis. I don't know the numerical average, but it's in that range probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1173, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to abandon this topic as well with regard to convoys. We have to go back to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Banbury, we established and you, yourself, confirmed that you interpreted the mandate of UNPROFOR to your colleagues; right?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, not a formal legal interpretation but a political one and as it applied to a certain context or situation that may have existed at various times in the -- during the course of the war, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was that mandate fully clear to you?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were certain ambiguities in the Security Council resolutions as a result of political divisions within the council and perhaps other reasons, and as a result, the resolutions from the council assigning UNPROFOR its mandate were themselves not always clear on all matters. So the -- there was a built-in lack of clarity in certain respects to UNPROFOR's mandate, so it was not always clear to anyone. It was impossible to be clear because of ambiguous language in the resolutions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D3368, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a letter of Mr. Akashi. He is writing to Mr. Annan on the 20th of May, 1995. It has to do with the implementation of the mandate of UNPROFOR, and it says: [In English] "Changes in the body of report have been highlighted for your ease of reference. The observations section has been significantly revised and should replace our previous draft."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please focus on this. I don't have time to read all of it so could you focus at least on paragraph 3, where Mr. Akashi says what all the ambiguities are. [In English] "UNPROFOR's mandate was further complicated by resolutions that refer to Chapter 7 for security and freedom of movement without clearly addressing the practical ramifications. Finally, the safe area mandate of the council contained in Resolution 836, and particularly its reliance on air power in response to attacks, has brought the force to the edge of an almost untenable balance between its impartiality as a basically peacekeeping operation and the use of force. As a result, UNPROFOR is currently constrained by the nature and the complexity of its mission, their contradictions and forces available to implement them." [Interpretation] Is that right? This is actually what you were speaking about earlier, some of the things you were talking about earlier about, these ambiguities, is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at page 5, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] "The Security Council in authorising UNPROFOR's initial mandate and deployment to Bosnia and Herzegovina did not contemplate an enforcement role. Authority for the use of force did not, therefore, go beyond the right of self-defence inherent to any United Nations peacekeeping force. The requirement to use force only within the confines of conventional peacekeeping principles and practices was also a direct and unavoidable consequence of UNPROFOR's tasks and deployment on the ground." [Interpretation] And so on and so forth. [In English] "The safe operations had, therefore, to be sought through adherence by all parties to a mutually acceptable agreement." [Interpretation] And in paragraph 11, in the middle: [In English] "Despite the constantly precarious status in deliveries to eastern enclaves and Sarajevo, where the problems of access, including the air-lift and airdrops, are intimately linked with the military situation on the grounds. The delivery of humanitarian assistance by UNHCR was, and continues to be, generally successful. This success can be attributed to the intensive negotiations with, and practical co-operation of, the parties on the delivery of humanitarian assistance. During periods of conflict, the use of humanitarian assistance" --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] "... as a weapon of war has been most apparent through denial of clearance," and so and so on. [Interpretation] Could you please look at paragraph 12. Paragraph 12 talks about Chapter 7 in the context of security of UNPROFOR. And then of paragraph 13, at the bottom, states: [In English] "And the subsequent resolutions cited above did not create new task for UNPROFOR or modify its rule of engagement since it stated previously the normal rule of engagement for all peacekeeping missions permit the use of force in self-defence." [Interpretation] Do you remember -- I am sorry the interpreter does not have the original text. I will try to be more careful. Do you remember, Mr. Banbury, that in our talks with General Rose, we clarified that close air support was an action aimed at defending the forces of the United Nations that had fallen into difficulties and that we accepted that, and that an air-strike is a measure of punishment --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic please repeat the end of that sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: -- which we do not accept?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The interpreters couldn't hear the last part of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We received an explanation that close air support meant support to UNPROFOR units that had fallen into difficulties and we accepted that, that was accepted by us. On the other hand, air-strikes were punitive measure that we never accepted. We gave our consent for the presence of United Nations that would imply interfering in the war. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The text that you cited from the document displayed is more comprehensive and deals with much more than just the issue of close air support and use of air-strikes. To address only your question, I agree, yes, that you and your authorities did distinguish between the use of close air support for the self-defence of UNPROFOR personnel and air-strikes against Bosnian Serb military targets that were not directly linked to self-defence action. I do not recall you ever agreeing with the concept of close air support, while -- although you did distinguish between the two. I also do not agree that the air-strikes were ever punitive in nature. They were meant to achieve specific military aim. They were not punitive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you have five minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was counting on that. I'm going to have one more document. And with a lot of regret, I will have to conclude this cross-examination. Can we now look at page 7, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 15 here talks about these areas, how these areas would need to be treated as safe areas but that the concept of those safe areas is not defined. [In English] "There was no enforcement component to the safe areas concept at its inception."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you look at this highlighted section: [In English] "While air power provides an indispensable factor of deterrence and should ideally be used in a graduated escalatory response to attacks as a last resort, experience has shown that using force against only one party, whether directly or through regional arrangements, alters the perception of the party on the neutrality of UNPROFOR. As the role of the UNPROFOR and UNHCR are often perceived as one, it becomes inevitable that their personnel are identified with the military intervention and perceived as a party to the war. The lightly armed, widely dispersed troops," and so on. [Interpretation] Do you remember that a week after this, NATO executed mass strategic strikes at Serb positions which then resulted in our capturing of UNPROFOR members?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we please -- well, unfortunately I don't have time for the entire document, but the entire document is available to the parties. I would like to tender this document and then move to the last document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Exhibit D1174.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I now have 1D3479, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And I would like to give you an example, an illustration from your statement where my -- it is unacceptable to me how you interpret the gist of the document. I don't have anything against the actual gist, but against your interpretation of it. You said, didn't you, in your statement --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am sorry, 1D2461.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 1D2461.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you said that I said that if the arms embargo is lifted we would attack UNPROFOR; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's not the exact quote but that was the gist of statement, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I say that I said that we were going to allow UNPROFOR to pull out through our territory, that we have nothing against the lifting of the arms embargo because the embargo didn't exist anyway, and that we would make it possible for UNPROFOR to withdraw safely. And then at another occasion, I said that we would consider foreigners unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the second part of paragraph 2, please. Can we scroll up a little bit. [In English] "Any such major offensive by his side would clearly make the lifting of the arms embargo inevitable as the world would not tolerate such a serious attack on the territory of B&H. Another consequence would be the termination of the UNPROFOR peacekeeping mission. As there was likely to be resistance to the withdrawal of UNPROFOR by the Muslims, it would be safer for the isolated units of UNPROFOR in the enclaves to withdraw from former Yugoslavia through Bosnian Serb-held territory. His forces would assist the passage of UNPROFOR as they did not want our weapons or equipment to fall into the hands of the BH Army." [Interpretation] Do you remember that this happened, that we made it possible for British troops to pull out from Gorazde before the bombing through Serbian territory?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall what troop movement you are referring to. There were troop movements in and out of Gorazde on -- across time, so I'm sorry, I don't recall specifically what you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, we will remind you. But is it not a fact here that I did not threaten UNPROFOR forces over the lifting of the arms embargo and over their possible withdrawal, but that I actually offered assistance? Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not believe I was at the meeting that is characterised in the document that is displayed. I accept that the document reflects an overall picture of what was stated at the meeting, including your position with respect to the possible lifting of the arms embargo in Bosnia. I do not believe that that changes my earlier statement or the information I have in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But this is opposite of what you said in your statement, that we would consider them as enemies and attack UNPROFOR if they pull out. But let's look at the following page to see when I exactly said that we would consider foreigners as adversaries. Paragraph 8: [In English] "Dr. Karadzic replied that if any more UNSCRs were passed against the Bosnian Serbs, then they would regard UNPROFOR as an adversary." [Interpretation] The way you see it and the way you interpret our position, obviously we are talking about the position stated at this meeting, you thought that we would consider UNPROFOR an adversary if the arms embargo was lifted and such an assertion is very detrimental to the Defence, but in essence, it is erroneous. And we are showing this document and indicating that the interpretation of the document is actually drastically different. Isn't that right? And I would like the parties to look at paragraph 58: [In English] "In the event the arms embargo was lifted, the Serbs would take UN blue helmets hostage, shoot down a lot of planes and arrest all foreigners."

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I was simply quoting a statement where you had been quoted. I was not conveying my opinion. It's not my interpretation. I was just factually reporting something that you were reported to have said. I think it's possible that you may have said one thing in one context and something different in a different context.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, can we have that document then? I have stated what is said in this document, I never said anything else, Mr. Banbury. I need to clarify each one of these 240 paragraphs and to see why the interpretation you provide is different from the map. Is the map different from the terrain?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we call up that document so that we can see whether that arises from that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's time to conclude, wrap up your cross-examination. We'll admit this document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1175, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it you have concluded, Mr. Karadzic. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I'm sorry to disturb you but I'm wondering if I could be heard very briefly on the issue of time and reconsideration. In particular, we absolutely have no time to deal with the count 11, and I would like to give you five points that are contained in this witness's notebooks about count 11 and let you decide whether you think that's valuable enough to have the cross-examination continue as a very specific example because these proceedings are basically being conducted very exemplary, but it would be a shame to simply lose the ability to defend on part of the case that is less important than others by not having enough time. So if you would allow me, outside of the presence of the witness, I would like to point to five points about count 11 that we simply didn't have time to get to and that I would ask that you consider giving him the time to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was it not your client's choice not to ask those questions? He had ample time asking other questions. I will consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Banbury, if you could excuse yourself for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, getting back to your question, your comment before, I just say there has to be choices made when there's time limitations, and count 11 -- there's consequences of count 11 that are considerably less than the other counts and so I don't think it was an irrational choice for Dr. Karadzic to leave that to the end. In any event, on the 24th of May, 1995, this witness attended a meeting and recorded in his notebooks that Admiral Smith was thinking of hitting -- doing the air-strikes tomorrow using laser-guided bombs. You will be called upon in this case to make a credibility assessment between testimony of General Smith who said that they had no capability to use a laser-guided weapons for the air-strikes and witness B, who we will call in our Defence case who we've presented already his affidavit showing that he was working on the ground as a forward air controller in Pale at the time these bombs were dropped, and this is some evidence that would support the Defence contention on this issue that you'll have to decide for credibility. It's in his notebook. It's an entry, we don't think it's suitable for bar table without giving the witness a chance to explain that entry. That's one example. Another example is that on the 26th of May, at a meeting, after they noted that there were three violations of the exclusion zone, two by the Bosnian Muslim Army and one by the Bosnian Serb Army, Mr. Akashi said that Secretary Albright was upset at their intention to strike the Bosnian Muslim Army. And so as we know, only air-strikes were made against the Serbs, which we contend is part of the equation as to why Dr. Karadzic believed that they had become combatants as opposed to simple peacekeepers. On the 27th of May, 1995, this witness noted in his notes of a meeting that the force commander, General Janvier said that the problem with the weapon collections points was that the circumstances in which the weapons could be used were never defined. That supports Dr. Karadzic's position that when this was negotiated, there was a belief by the Serbs that they could take out these weapons when they were attacked or when they needed them for defensive purposes. And we've had uncontradicted evidence that in the middle of May there was a Bosnian Muslim offensive, which would once again tend to support the Defence contention that the UN had become belligerents. On the 29th of May, this witness noted that General Janvier said that the talks between the UN and the Bosnian Serb Army concerning the exchange of prisoners had been interrupted. This would be the first confirmation that there was on the UN side a negotiations for the exchange of the four prisoners that they had taken on the Vrbanja bridge, an event which would make them equally responsible for hostage taking as Bosnian Serbs, since hostage taking is defined as the placing of a condition upon the release or a harm coming to a person in their custody. And finally, on the 2nd of June, 1995, this witness noted in his notebooks that Fred Eckhart had reported that the Bosnian Muslim General Divjak had said that NATO had chosen their target well, that the Serb attacks on Sarajevo had been impacted by the attack on the Pale ammunition depot, and that the Serbs would need 15 to 30 days to resupply from Serbia, which again supports the Defence contention that the UN had become part of the belligerents and combatants as opposed to a neutral party. So those are examples of cross-examination that simply weren't reached and I would ask that you give us time to be able to do that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, what sort of period of time are you suggesting, realistically rather than, as it were, optimistically.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I think for -- those five points could be covered in about 30 minutes, perhaps less, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Perhaps less?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I think I could do it in about 15 minutes but I was giving Dr. Karadzic a cushion, so perhaps less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Perhaps Dr. Karadzic would borrow your cushion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, do you by any chance know whether Mr. Banbury will be available tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: He could be available for a period of time in the morning, but he is due and required back in New York later on in the day tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Banbury, I apologise for your inconvenience. Given the importance of your evidence as well as the subject matter raised by Mr. Robinson, the Chamber has decided to allow the accused to have additional half an hour tomorrow morning, so my question to you is whether you would be available tomorrow morning for about less than an hour in the morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, in the interests of fairness to the accused and justice, I'd be happy to be available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I appreciate it very much. We'll rise today and resume tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 17th day of March, 2011, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.28 p.m.,
